speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to discussion of a serious matter.
Since the Department of National Health and Welfare has decided to enclose messages of public interest with family allowance and old age pension cheques, and since it is likely that other departments will want to use the same tactic, we have a right to question the trend of these messages.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Godin):
That this House require all so-called messages of public interest to be sent out to Canadians by the Department of National Health and Welfare under the same cover as family allowance and old age pension cheques, or by any other federal department to accompany routine correspondence, to be first examined by the appropriate standing committee for approval, amendment or rejection, in order that the messages may in no instance be employed to any end other than the objective information of Canadians.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to set aside the first week in May as national hire the handicapped week. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of the Environment. In view of the minister's statement to James MacKenzie of the Globe and Mail on Friday last that Canada and the United States have agreed to set up a joint working committee for both east and west coasts to discuss aids to shipping and environmental protection, can he tell the House whether in fact a joint committee has been established, whether that committee has in fact ever met and, if so, has it submitted any report to the respective governments?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-INQUIRY AS TO CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE TO DISCUSS ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION-CANADIAN PROPOSALS
speechtext: Order, please. The Chair will allow the minister to reply, but perhaps I should indicate to the hon. member that it is not regular or in order to ask a question based on a statement made by a minister outside the House. The rule is clear that such statements made outside the House can be brought into the discussion only to the extent that a member may want to ask the Prime Minister whether such a statement represents government policy. We might assume that the question has been asked without reference to the statement made outside the House and the minister can reply on that basis.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Davis (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-INQUIRY AS TO CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE TO DISCUSS ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION-CANADIAN PROPOSALS
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. The word "committee" is inappropriate. However, there have been meetings and there will continue to be meetings between myself and Mr. Russell Train, who is the presidential adviser in Washington on environmental matters. We did meet last April, we met again in July and we are scheduled to meet again early next month on matters of the nature of pollution on both our coasts. I might add that officials from Canada and the U.S. are meeting and studying problems on both coasts, but there is no ministerial committee.

It was a committee which had been suggested by President Nixon as a counter-proposal to our request that this matter be sent to the IJC.
I want to ask the Minister of the Environment whether or not the committee which was suggested by President Nixon is to be set up or whether in fact there is to be no committee and the government has no intention of pressing to have a committee set up to deal with the very serious problem of tankers coming down the British Columbia coast from Valdez to Cherry Point?

subtopic: PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-INQUIRY AS TO CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE TO DISCUSS ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION-CANADIAN PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the sequence as I recall it is this: About a year ago Canada was pressing for a Canada-U.S. reference to the International Joint Commission concerning the matter of tankers on the west coast and the possibility of oil pollution in Puget Sound and the Gulf of Georgia area. The response of the United States was negative. President Nixon, as I recall it, however, suggested as an alternative that a committee be established at the ministerial level. Our response was that we might better proceed in the manner I have reported, namely, the Minister of the Environment for Canada working with Mr. Train of the United States.

subtopic: PROPOSED WEST COAST OIL TANKER ROUTE-INQUIRY AS TO CANADA-UNITED STATES COMMITTEE TO DISCUSS ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION-CANADIAN PROPOSALS

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to conclude my remarks on the government's proposal to increase old age assistance. On Friday last I said the sum was grossly inadequate. You may remember, Mr. Speaker, that at that time the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) rose to correct a passage in Hansard, in which he was reported as saying that the government had effectively banished poverty for the aged in this country. He said he did not say that, and I believe him when he says he did not say that. Yet, obviously, somebody in the government thought it, Mr. Speaker, because that text did not appear in Hansard by accident. Obviously, somebody deep in the mushroom cellars under the headquarters of the Department of National Health and Welfare wrote those words. There is a cabal that believes that this government has effectively banished poverty for people over the age of 65. They committed those thoughts to paper, but fortunately the minister was embarrassed enough by their ever-eagerness to do us the honour of correcting his remarks, substituting a somewhat less offensive piece of governmental braggadocio. Nevertheless, he doubtless believes that the government has done a good job for our old people.
So, obviously, do my hon. friends to the south of us in this chamber. I should like to dwell for a few moments on some of the remarks that the members of that party have made. Their leader, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), said during the debate on the budget that he thought that my leader had "lost his marbles"; I think that was the phrase he used. I want to quote to you, Mr. Speaker, something that the leader of the New Democratic Party-or should I say the not so new and not so democratic party-said. I hear hon. members to my far
Old Age Security Act
left crying "Oh!". The leader of the New Democratic Party said during the budget debate that he suspected my party were so hungry for power that they would vote for the communist manifesto. I suggest to them that if they had to, in order to keep this government in power, they would almost vote for the Regina manifesto. They have turfed out of their party everyone who laid claim to believing in the philosophy of socialism which they are supposed to espouse. Anybody who is young and a socialist has no place in the councils of the NDP; that is a matter of record so we do not have to debate it here.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, let me tell you about the statement that the hon. member for York South made during the election campaign, just one week before election day last October. He was in Victoria at the time and was talking about pensions. He said that his party, if it were elected, would immediately institute a pension plan raising the basic pension to $150 a month. He then said this: "You send a large number of NDP members to parliament and we'll make life hell for the Trudeau government". During my education I studied under Jesuits, among others, and sometimes they were at pains to describe to us the tortures of hell. They frightened me, since I was a young boy at the time; in fact, they scared the hell out of me. But I can say that I have not seen any members of this woefully inadequate government across the way suffering torment of any kind at the hands of the New Democratic Party, least of all the torment of hell.
The fact is that the leader of the New Democratic Party, who accused my leader of losing his marbles, may be in need of a little geriatric assistance. I am not going to accuse him of having lost his marbles or of having his mental faculties in any way diminished by his great age, but I would suggest to him that sometimes one's sight begins to play tricks with one when one reaches a certain age, and that the Trudeau government is over on that side, not on this side where most of his invective has been directed.
If he and his party really want to see a pension that is better than the one now being put up by the Liberal government, I suggest that they defeat the government and let another election take place. We do not want the help of that rag, tag and bobtail minority down there. We do not want to form a government that depends daily for its existence on a little blowhard minority with no mandate. What we want is an end to a situation in which this parliament can be frustrated in its attempt to get on with things because of the fact that this little group of 31 members, fully one-third of whom are here by virtue of victories consisting of less than 2,000 votes plurality, has the misplaced and I submit misused power to impose its will on the crippled giant across the way.
These members tell us that daily they are shoring up the government because they want to see programs passed that are good for the people. I am not at all surprised to hear them say this, but I did go back over my files today and I found that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has long held the view that co-operation with the Liberals is a defensible philosophy for a New Democratic Party politician to profess. In fact, back in 1965 there was a scandal within the NDP caucus in this House of the most serious proportions. It seems that the

caucus at that time became very cross with the hon. member and wanted to remove him as House leader. There was a special caucus meeting held to discuss this proposition, and the reason they gave for this meeting was that the hon. member was too helpful to Liberals.
The hon. member has been quoted on many occasions- the most recent I have been able to find was in January last, but he is on record as long ago as 1965-as saying that he thinks minority government is the best kind of government. He believes that under that system more will be done for the Canadian people than if there is a majority government, though he makes one very important reservation, of course, which is unless a majority government be formed by him and his colleagues. So in that principle as in all others we find there are two sides to the question and that it depends very much upon whose ox has been gored. All of us who are in politics have compromised from time to time. But the amusing and sometimes bemusing thing about the NDP is that while they are in the process of making their tortuous and painful circumlocutions to arrive at B when they left A, they will never admit that they have done so and become very cross indeed when anyone accuses them of that. Thus it was that the leader of that party, having committed his party members to vote for the budget, said he was doing so because the budget contained no concessions to industry. How he arrived at that conclusion, of course, I shall leave the House to decide; I cannot imagine how he could possibly arrive at such a conclusion.
I am sure hon. members will be pleased to hear that I have just about reached the end of my speech. May I merely conclude by saying that we do not believe that a $100 pension is enough. I hold that view to the extent that I cannot vote for this proposal. It is my intention-and I hope I will be joined by members of the House from all parties-to continue to work as hard as I can, in common with members like the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), who has worked all his parliamentary career to this end, to better the lot of the pensioners. Those who snigger at this, Mr. Speaker, merely betray their total ignorance of what has been happening here over the past few years. I intend to join forces with that hon. member and other members who have concern for the old people of this country in order to try to make sure they receive, before too many months go by, an amount of money that will enable them to live in the peace, dignity and harmony that they deserve, having worked hard and carried this country on their backs for all their working lives.

I would remind the hon. member of the Conservative party publication entitled "Policies and Commitments" dated September, 1972, which did not even contain a chapter with regard to pensions. At page 52 under the heading of "Poverty" there is the statement that the Tories would maintain the present plans and remove the 2 per cent ceiling on the cost of living adjustment. At that time the old age pension was $82.88, and the Conservative party did not even know that the Liberal government had taken off the 2 per cent ceiling in respect of the cost of living adjustment. This is the program the Conservative party presented to the people during the election. The leader of the party has attempted since to say it could be inferred from his speeches that the old age pension under the Tories would have been between $90 and $95. We then heard the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), the main spokesman for that party on pensions, say many things, but not one word regarding that the Conservative party would do concerning pensions. He said not one word as to the amount.

speechtext:
The hon. member said that the 1973 pension should be $107, but there was not one word in respect of what the Conservative party would do concerning the amount of the pension. I think it would be fair to say that
1,800,000	senior citizens are delighted with the changes contained in the legislation, and I want to commend the minister for bringing it forward. I recall that before he was a member or a minister he was the grey eminence behind the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He had a keen, analytical mind and a bureaucratic approach to political problems. After listening to his speech introducing the changes I now realize he is intellectually strong, decidedly competent, deeply sensitive, compassionate and strongly determined to take care of senior citizens.
Much the same can be said about the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). He has been a crusader, a man of convictions, a man of concern and a man of compassion. When he spoke as the spokesman for

March 8, 1973

our party he set forth the historical and philosophical development of pensions. Many of us, after hearing his speech, felt that he was a man Canadians have grown to respect and admire for his fine contributions to social legislation for pensioners. I just noticed one of the members leave. I imagine he is most embarrassed at the position and policy of his party concerning pensions.
This legislation indicates that the Prime Minister and his party got the message of October 30, 1972. I feel that the people of Canada are the main beneficiaries of minority governments, and that it is fair to say many Canadians applaud the decision of the New Democratic Party, announced shortly after the election, that we would support the government in power, be it Liberal or Tory, provided progressive legislation was brought forth to the benefit of all people in Canada.
On January 4 the Liberals did bring forth a Speech from the Throne which contained many promises concerning pensions, housing and foreign ownership. We in the NDP supported the government on the basis that an opportunity should be given the government to translate its promises into legislation. Then, on February 19, the Liberals brought forth a budget which contained certain goodies relating to tax cuts, an improvement in the pensions of senior citizens and veterans and cuts in respect of sales tax. That is why we in the NDP supported the government on the budget, even though we had certain reservations about expansionary measures in respect of unemployment.
What is the position of the Progressive Conservative party? Had we voted with them against the budget we would have deprived the people of Canada of all those benefits derived from it. I said in my opening remarks that the Conservatives never stated that they would give an increase. In fact, not one word has been forthcoming from any of their speakers in respect of the amount of the increase to pensioners.

Again we must appreciate that the best effort of the Tories was $65 at 70 years of age, and I think the hon. member for Bruce (Mr. Whicher) had the right to mention that during the debate. The very best effort of the Conservative party was $65 per month at age 70. The payment of $100 basic old age pension and the combined OAS and GIS of $170 with a payment of $325 to a married couple represent a step in the right direction.
Somebody asked what we in the NDP would do. We stated clearly that our position was related to an amount
Old Age Security Act
of $150 on the principle of universality. We have stated many times that this would do away with divisiveness and administrative complexity-and I refer to the combined OAS and GIS-being brought about concerning pensions.
I	would remind hon. members that the NDP government in British Columbia has ensured that every pensioner will get a minimum of $200 a month. This indicates that even though we are tied to $150 in respect of basic old age security pensions, we are prepared to move to take care of Canadians who are finding it difficult to meet expenses today. We feel, and I am sure the last speaker will bring this to the attention of the province of Ontario, that the government of Ontario should ensure that every pensioner in this province gets a minimum of $200. I had thought my good friend would make this type of remark concerning pensions, rather than attack his friends to the left.
The minister, when he spoke, set forth the figures which showed that 500,000 pensioners were in receipt of the full old age pension and guaranteed income supplement, and that another 550,000 were in receipt of partial OAS and GIS while 750,000 were in receipt of OAS alone, the basic pension. This indicates the three different groups of pensioners we have in this country today. He also pointed out that the provinces have established priorities with regard to other groups in the community such as the disabled, single family parents, unemployable unemployed, and low income people. He quite rightly pointed out that the Canada Assistance Plan provides a measure of relief to the provinces which are participating in it because of the 50 per cent contribution by the federal government. This type of comment is justified and constructive, but I think there is a necessity for the federal government to establish priorities concerning the unemployed, inflation and social security measures.
In respect of senior citizens, I think the priority at the moment, after the passage of this legislation, should be, first, in relation to housing. There should be more senior citizens' housing so that the senior citizens can rent housing at reasonable rates. This would mean that any increases that they are now receiving would not be swallowed up through increases in rent. Also if we were to increase the amount of housing available for senior citizens we would probably have a practical demonstration of what the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) called the trickled-down theory in housing, whereby senior citizens who now occupy large homes might move to more comfortable accommodation and avoid the necessity of looking after repairs, painting and so on. If they so wished, such persons could move into senior citizens accommodation and thus provide more homes for younger families. I believe it is very important that more senior citizens housing be constructed.
Another priority for our senior citizens would be the provision of drugs at reasonable prices. I recall that when the government eliminated the 11 per cent sales tax on drugs many people thought we would have a substantial reduction in the price of drugs. This did not happen. In fact, studies indicate that some drug firms absorbed that
II	per cent and put it into their pockets. I would remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the province of Manitoba, under a New Democratic Party government, brought forward its

March 8, 1973
Old Age Security Act
budget a short time ago in which provision was made for free drugs for all senior citizens. This is a measure which I think should be promoted by the federal government in an attempt to spur on the other provinces to take action concerning drugs for our senior citizens.
The next item of priority in respect of senior citizens should involve food costs. Some protection should be given to the Price of basic foods enjoyed by senior citizens. An article in the Toronto Star of February 26 by Anne Wanstall indicates how the sudden hikes in prices have affected many people. She said:
Supermarkets are first in line as consumers fire pot shots that could grow into cannon balls. If last week's mail is anything to go by, the executives who make the policies which determine the prices we're asked to pay, had better come up with some answers.
Then, she gave an example:
Wanda Pratt of Weston has a gripe about the rising price of prune juice. "About six weeks ago I paid 39 cents. Then it went up to 42 cents; two weeks later up to 49 cents and last week to 52 cents. They can't tell me that this was all due to a poor crop of plums."
She points out that this purchase poker that the chain stores play with regard to food prices must stop because it directly affects different groups within the community. One group which is substantially affected is the senior citizens.
Another priority in respect of the senior citizens I think should involve the situation where one spouse is under 65 years of age. In his speech the minister indicated that the cost of granting a pension to a person who is between age 60 and age 64 while the other person is over age 65 would be $150 million. I suggest this would be an expense well worth incurring, since there are many cases in which one pensioner is over age 65 while the other is under age 65. These people suffer severe hardships today. When we think that we are contemplating giving an amount of $500 million to corporations through tax benefits, surely we can give an amount of $150 million to the senior citizens in order to cover that situation.
I believe the government should also consider as a priority the lowering of the age in respect of pensions to 60 years. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that the test may have to be that of employment. There is a great deal of unemployment at the moment and many people feel that the lowering of the pensionable age to 60 on a voluntary rather than a compulsory basis would draw out many workers who are now 60 years of age and over.
I recall the experience I had in Toronto. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was kind enough to send me as a representative of our party to a pension conference. At that conference I put forward the suggestion that we should lower the age limit to 60 years. I received an interesting answer from one of the senior citizens. She asked me if I agreed that Senators and Members of Parliament should quit work at age 60. She wanted to know why I was asking them to quit when Senators and Members of Parliament continue for many years beyond age 60.1 am inclined to agree with her point. It underlines the necessity of retirement at that age being voluntary rather than compulsory. The adoption of this proposal would involve the lowering of the eligible age in

respect of the Canada Pension Plan, and some of the other pension funds, because it would not do to have a person retire at age 60 and receive merely the basic old age pension, plus perhaps the guaranteed income supplement, and then have to wait until age 65 before receiving benefit under the Canada Pension Plan. That is one problem. The other problem is that we would have to include an acceleration clause in the Canada Pension Plan in the same way it is incorporated in the old age security plan. This should be a requirement. Otherwise, the amount of pension received by people when they retire will be reduced substantially as a result of the increase in the cost of living.
These are the three areas to which the government should give first priority for study, research and development of policy. We in the NDP welcome the changes in the legislation, but we look forward to further improvements in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to seize this opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-147.
I do not rise to fight this bill, but to approve it. We do not have the chance to approve stronger measures, so we shall at least give our approval to the minimum and we hope the bill will have third reading as soon as possible. That is why we do not wish unduly to delay the committee stage of the bill.
In this connection, I wonder why it should be referred to committee; we might just as well complete the second and third readings right away, and say: That's that, the bill is passed, for I cannot see what major amendments the committee could make. Some amendments will be proposed, but since amendments increasing government expenditure cannot be made in committee, I see no compelling reason why the bill should go to committee. Still, procedure must be followed, even if it does take time. We must reply to those who ask when the bill will go through, saying: Wait for the procedure to take its course.
It has always struck me in the House that, when any government introduces some social reform, they always make it seem to the people like some wonderful bargain that they had not been expecting. When you get down to studying it, there is really very little to it.
The process is reversed when it comes to proposed taxation. They speak quite bashfully to the public, and say: Well, it isn't much really. Just a little tax that you will hardly feel at all; whereas in fact it is a monstrosity. This is the sleight of hand that they try out on the public. What I dislike is the dishonesty of it.
Why not call on the population and simply say: This is what we have to offer. The government should stop playing cat and mouse with the people. After all, they are not at all more stupid than we are. Everybody can see through the government's game and this is why today they hate only some methods of the government. In fact, those methods have always been used.
The bill before us will increase the pension to $100 a month. First of all, they say that the pension is being raised from $82 to $100, which is not true since by the end
March 8, 1973

of March the pension will automatically fall to $86.61. The increase coming into force on April 1 amounts to only $13.39 a month. Once more, let us speak the truth. I like things to be clear and I do support truth. This is why I wish to quote the appropriate figures very clearly.
Many politicians deliberately tell people in their faces: the pension will amount to $170. This is another story that proves false. The pension does not amount to $170 but to $100 a month, and to this sum can be added a $70 supplement-I call that public assistance-subject to all kinds of inquiries whose purpose is to try to avoid granting it. Mr. Speaker, while adding a $70 supplement, they do not intend to do justice to the older citizens because the purpose of all these inquiries is to try to avoid granting it. Therefore, let us not call that a pension.
When referring to the pension in the House, I always have said: The pension, to be fair and equitable, must first of all be universal. If we allege that the pension amounts to $170, let us grant it to everybody indiscriminately. We should not make the senior citizens believe that they will receive monthly pensions of $170 because if they have another income their pensions are decreased. Therefore, what they are told is not true. Personally I simply tell them: Your pension is now $82 and it will be raised to $100. The rest of the pension can vary since what you get will depend on your income.
Those who have worked hard during their lifetime to save some money-it was the practice of our fathers and grandfathers for their old days-made a mistake. Because they have saved a few hundred dollars they will not get the $70 supplement. They are penalized by the government for their foresight. Today wealth means getting into debt and you must be old and in debt to receive the odd favour from the government. This seems to be the kind of education that we are trying to give today to our youth and I think it is very, very bad.
We simply ask for a pension. If we have again an opportunity to discuss that question in committee, we shall again ask for a true pension of $170 and 100 per cent universal for all senior citizens. When I say "all senior citizens" I mean the spouse younger than her pensionned husband. I always understood that when a pension is paid to the husband it is a family pension and if his wife is younger she is entitled to this pension.
We cannot expect an elderly couple to live five years on the salary of a single person. And I am very surprised that the government has not understood this fact because before the budget was introduced I was really sure that the pensioner's spouse was going to be eligible for the new pension. But it is not so, we still remain in the same old rut, we keep the same old principles and we leave the spouse aside and without any income.
The spouse may have some income in some provinces but not in Quebec. As soon as the husband gets $170, the Quebec Department of Health will tell him: that is enough. In Quebec, two persons must be satisfied with $170 to make a living. What a bright reasoning. These couples will have to fight again, beg and implore small politically bred inspectors to see if they have not inherited a few hundred dollars. We are against such ways of pro-
Old Age Security Act
ceeding and this is why I say and repeat that only when the pension is universal will elder people begin to be treated as they deserve.
Secondly, like the New Democratic Party we often advocated in this House lowering the eligibility for pensions to age 60. I suggest this would be a very interesting matter of debate in committee, because bringing the age down to 60 does not require any effort on the part of the government and we offer them a means to really fight unemployment. As a matter of fact, according to some research I did at Statistics Canada, if we allowed people aged 60 to 65 to retire, we would provide 400,000 new jobs, which would enable 400,000 heads of families who now depend on the public treasury, who have 5, 6, 7 or 8 children and who cost the two levels of government $400, $500 or more a month, to go and earn a living in industry and take the place of the people who could retire if they were given $325 a month.
Mr. Speaker, the two levels of government would thus save money, in addition to which there would be 400,000 fewer unemployed. That is why we have suggested that pensionable age be reduced to 60; it would help the government solve the unemployment problem. Frankly, I am surprised again today that the government has not even mentioned it.
I do not know whether it is being discussed at the ministerial level but I feel this would be the best thing; let us stop applying bandaids to reduce unemployment, ban-daids such as LIP projects, municipal projects, to create employment. A small political bonus is given industry; then we are told that 200 jobs have been created. That is not true; often, 200 jobs were wiped out. There is a bit of political play and we are told that will solve the problem of unemployment; that is not true.
Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the problem of unemployment will only be solved through a massive movement of workers. As for senior citizens between 60 and 65, they should be given real instead of sham pensions. Thus,
400,000	unemployed heads of families could earn a living in industry and there would be only 300,000 unemployed left.
In addition, a salary should be paid to mothers. In that case, according to a survey 200,000 mothers would reintegrate their home, and there would be 200,000 fewer unemployed.
These are all suggestions, Mr. Speaker, that we make to the government so that it try and solve this famous unemployment problem. Once again, it is not by trying all kinds of little political tricks that a solution will be found to this unemployment problem. Everything that is done is unfair. Cases of injustice are multiplied by political patronage.
Mr. Speaker, once again, I greatly appreciate the little we are getting today; we shall give our full support to the bill but we truly hope that the government will propose within a few months a more concrete, more realistic bill that will enable it to deal with the unemployment problem.
We also would have liked the bill to provide for an agreement on drugs with the provinces. Today, the big problem of senior citizens aged 65 and over is that of drugs. They require so much care and so many drugs that

March 8, 1973
Old Age Security Act
when they have to pay, life is not a bed of roses in many homes.
In my riding, I had the opportunity to visit most of the homes for the aged and I think that their problem is one of drugs.
If, one day, we could give them such things as drugs, as we do for welfare recipients, this would lessen a great deal the worries of senior citizens. We would thus find a solution to another problem facing these people.
I do not know what the situation is outside the province of Quebec, but I am telling the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to be on the lookout, because Quebecers are often being tricked. Every time an increase was granted, Quebec hurried to get it back right away and this is expected to happen again. It has already started in the case of rents and it is going to happen in nursing homes, Mr. Speaker. In such cases, older people suddenly realize that they are poorer than before, after a bill is passed, because the moment the government is giving people more money to improve their lot, the Quebec government sends out two or three inspectors to recover this money for the benefit of the provincial treasury.
It is too bad it's happening in my own province, but I must say it and I have to warn the minister about this.
We are in favour of this bill and we do not want to delay it being referred to the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express a few comments on this very important bill. At the time of the budget debate, I had, like many others, the opportunity to voice a few opinions about old age security.
As this bill provides for a substantial increase in the income of older people, I am sorry that consideration was not given to granting the old age security pension to people under 65.
I would have believed it possible to give the old age security pension to the persons of 64 at least, for the present year. I think that many hon. members have already addressed this request to the minister in this House. I presume that the minister responsible and his officials have looked into the matter of reducing the eligibility age for old age pensions.
In view of the present social situation and the technical changes which have occurred in industry, there is an urgent need to give to people of 60 years of age and over a well deserved retirement. I am not the first one to draw the Minister's attention to the unemployment situation in the country. Personally, I feel that it would be a great help toward alleviating this problem which has been with us for several years and that it could allow people of 60 and over to receive the pension even though we may extend the process over a five-year period as we did before when the eligibility age for the old age security pension was lowered from 70 to 65.
I believe that this would have been possible and I worry a little about the attitude of parties in general which could not get together and force the government to take such a step. I am thinking particularly of NDP members who,

since I came here at least, have many times expressed their interest in our senior citizens and underprivileged people. And I was very surprised that the NDP Party did not dare bring forward an amendment to that effect when the budget was tabled. I will not look for the reasons, because many members know them. However, I must remind the members of the New Democratic Party that they must respect the principles which they have always bravely upheld in this House and I wonder to what extent the public is aware not only of some kind of hesitation, but also of a certain amount of dishonesty in connection with the principles they have always extolled.
I think that the parties and members opposite would have surely been pleased to support an amendment brought in by the New Democratic Party and aimed at granting old age security pensions at least to people 64 years of age going down gradually to those 60 years of age. I take the liberty of reminding members of that party the position which they have always held in this House and may they also be reminded that the Canadian people are somewhat concerned about their inaction with respect to those principles.
Mr. Speaker, I would therefore like to take this opportunity, while admitting that the increases are most acceptable and interesting for our senior citizens, to remind the Minister of the importance of reconsidering-if this has not already been done-the possibility of enabling more people aged 60 or over to "go on leave". I would not go so far as saying that all those who could go on leave to-morrow morning, because of old age security pensions being granted at the early age of 60, should be replaced in industry. No, sir. For various reasons, I think that some industries would not hire other people to replace them. Still, I think that thousands of people could go into retirement and that jobs could be found for thousands of unemployed. Thus our present social context would be improved by allowing people aged 60 to go on leave and by having employment made available to 20-year-olds for whom the State often spends as much as $100 a week.
I feel that this should be considered by this House and also that it is important to remember all the efforts that this government has made during the past five years injecting money into various parts of this country, in order to fight unemployment; we find that in spite of all these efforts, the unemployment rate has increased twofold if not threefold. I therefore feel this measure would promote a healthy social atmosphere and once more I invite hon. members of this House to give serious thought to this possibility and to urge the government to take early action. In the present situation, this possibility exists. All opposition members can certainly join forces and impose such action on the government, should they hesitate too long.
I venture to believe that the minister will take these remarks into consideration, as well as those of previous speakers and will give a positive reply to those who anxiously look to this legislation. Furthermore, recently, in my riding, the Central Council of the CNTU, during its Convention, adopted a resolution which I communicated this week to the minister. On the basis of my prior representations concerning this legislation, I urge the minister to grant sixty year olds the old age security pension.
March 8, 1973

Furthermore, I do hope that if unions like the CNTU with a membership of thousands of workers are favourable to that legislation, it would be proper to give this old age security pension to all those who are 65.
I shall limit myself to these few remarks. I did not want to let this opportunity go by without asking again for the passing of a law which would provide the old age security pension to those who are 60.
And I would also invite the minister to consider the possibility of giving this pension to the spouse who has not yet reached the age of 65. It is absolutely unfair for a couple when both are over age 65 to get $325 while a senior citizen whose spouse is younger has to live on $170.
Since it is unfair, I feel it is imperative for the government to study seriously the possibility of giving more assistance to the couple who is inconvenienced and antagonized by an act that grants $325 to one couple and $170 to another.
I know that by proving to the department of National Health and Welfare that the couple's income is not sufficient, some compensation may be obtained. But I also know very well that several persons have a hard time proving their entitlement to those supplementary benefits, that are often necessary, and that it often takes months of inquiry for the department to recognize their right to them.
So I think that such injustice should be corrected and that these people should be reassured by enacting a legislation whch would be fairer and more flexible and which would allow us to solve a great number of problems.
I will conclude my remarks, in expressing the hope that the minister will take them into account and that the political parties which have the opportunity to bring the government to enact that solution will unite and that the New Democratic Party will not hesitate in following the principles they have always defended in this House.
As far as I am and many others are concerned, we entertain certain reservations about the honesty they have always displayed towards senior citizens. It is never too late to take action. I would hope that, the various parties in this House will combine their efforts, either in committee or through another way, to make it possible for the senior citizens to obtain that pension as soon as possible, or at least to get it on a five years trial basis as it has already been done in other circumstances.
That would really show that we want to do something that an effort is being made to solve the problems; I believe that it would be a very good step for the minister, the Government and the Parliament to take.

I must say that that question has been submitted to me very frequently by my Liberal colleagues since I have had the honour of assuming the responsibilities of Minister of National Health and Welfare.

March 8, 1973
Old Age Security Act
I would like to reassure hon. members that I am not opposed to it in principle, far from it. I hope I have shown in the speech I made at the beginning of the debate on second reading that I consider it my duty to look into that problem with my provincial colleagues in the light of an over-all reform of social security in Canada. As I indicated in that speech, we have over 150,000 abandoned mothers who must look after 350,000 children and who at the present time receive benefits which are a shame to this country and unworthy of the condition in which they find themselves.
There are also 200,000 disabled people in Canada, between ages 18 and 65, who are now getting much lower benefits than those paid to older people. There are also
575,000	persons under social security who are also getting much lower benefits than those paid to older people.
While considering the question of reducing the age of eligibility for pension benefits, we should look into the whole question of benefits that are paid to the needy in this country. It is not only a question of trying to solve the problem of people from 60 to 65 but of tackling the poverty issue in all its aspects. I believe this would be the best way for us to meet the expectations of all Canadian citizens and the best way for this parliament, I think, to overcome poverty problem which unfortunately is still too acute everywhere in Canada despite the wealth of this country.
I am pleased to note that the oppositions parties generally agree with the government and will support this bill. [English]

There is another aspect of this question that also surprises me about the attitude of the Conservative party in this matter. The hon. member asked the government for immediate action on this, even though he knew very well that I had stated quite clearly in this House that I have discussed this matter with my provincial counterparts. We were unanimously of the view that, at this particular time, we should not touch the structure of the system of old age security in this country, but that this question should be part of the general review that will take place of the social security system. They were not opposed in principle to reducing the age for benefits, but they said, "Before you go ahead and do that on your own, let us have a meeting; let us see what are the priorities in this country for the payment of social benefits, and let us see, together, whether the first priority should be lowering the age for the payment of pensions or whether the first priority should not be in other areas of welfare in this country." That is what the provinces said, all of them, including those in which the Conservative party happens to be in power.
The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) now says, "We want all this now." He is the same member who, during the campaign, went around accusing the government of rigidity, of not listening to the provinces, of acting on its own, of arrogance-you name it. That same hon. member and that same party to which he belongs, after having talked about co-operation with provinces, satisfying the provinces and what not, now come before the House and say, "Go ahead; act now; forget about the provinces; do not care about them." And on that account, the point raised by the hon. member who spoke on behalf of the Social Credit Party of Canada surely deserves notice.

Mr. Speaker, as far as the first question is concerned, I shall certainly be very pleased, if allowed to do so under the rules of the committee, to have a full discussion with hon. members on the question of lowering the age and all other aspects. Second, I want to assure hon. members that I do not have a closed mind on this question; I have a very open mind. I would love to be able to do this, but as I have mentioned we must look at the matter in terms of general priorities in the field of social security at the present time, taking into account the resources that may reasonably be made available in the short term.
With regard to action being taken in the present session, there will be further meetings with the provinces. I do not know whether the meeting being held in April will be sufficient to enable us to arrive at some agreement, or at some consensus, or whatever is the term we use for what we do with the provincial governments. If a consensus develops with the provinces that this is an area which should receive priority, then I would be happy to raise the matter with my colleagues and see whether we can take some action.
At the present time my view is that before committing ourselves to making any such move in the immediate future we should take a very careful and thorough look, not only at whether there should be a lowering of the age for pension entitlement but also at all of the calls that people in this country who are in need make upon the public purse, whether it be the federal purse or the provincial purse. As the hon. member knows, many demands are made on the provinces in the field of welfare for people below 65 years of age.
I am not in a position to commit the government or myself to taking action on this subject in this particular session of parliament. I have said that I feel that the next step to take in this session-and I do not know how many sessions there will be in this parliament-is to substantial-

ly improve the family allowance scheme. Can we then take a third step, which would be to decrease the age for pension entitlement during the course of this session? Personally, I would doubt it, but I have an open mind on the subject and will keep an open mind.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
that Bill C-148, to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be speaking at this time on a bill designed to improve the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. I should like first to recall briefly to the House some of the significant improvements which have been effected in the legislation governing war veterans allowances and civilian war allowances since January 1972.
On March 21, 1972, the regulations were amended so that exempt casual earnings were not restricted to a four month period.
On May 15, 1972, legislation was approved which exempted cost of living increases in the OAS and GIS payments in the amount of $15 for single war allowance recipients and $30 for married recipients.
On May 19, 1972, the War Veterans Allowance Act was amended to provide for escalation of the rates and ceilings effective January 1, 1972 and on January 1 of each succeeding year, in accordance with increases in the consumer price index.
On November 9, 1972, the regulation was removed which assessed as income for war veterans allowance and civilian war allowances purposes, a percentage of the value of a home in excess of $10,000.
On January 13, 1973, the amount of casual earnings permitted in any year was increased from $800 to $1000 for single recipients and from $1200 to $1500 for married recipients.
Finally, the war veterans allowance and civilian war allowances rates and ceilings which were in effect on December 31, 1971 have since been improved by $10 per month for single and $16.61 per month for married recipients.
The bill now before you will further increase these rates and ceilings by an additional $20.14 single and $39.60 married. This provides a total increase of $30.14 or 24.8 per cent, single, and $56.21 or 27.8 per cent, married, since December 31, 1971. The orphan rates have similarly been increased by more than 24 per cent during this 15-month period.
War Veterans Allowance Act
Another major feature of this bill is the removal of personal property limitations which now stand at $1250 single and $2500 married. This means that it will no longer be necessary for an applicant to liquidate his assets in order to qualify for an allowance.
I am especially pleased and proud to speak to this bill because, although rates and ceilings, casual earnings and permissible property values have changed many times since the War Veterans Allowance Act was passed in 1930, this is the first time a bill has been introduced in this House which proposes the complete removal of the limits on personal property. This will mean that war veterans allowances and civilian war allowances will, as of April 1, 1973, change from a means tested program to a modified income tested program.
I am sure all members will agree that those who are eligible to receive payments under these acts merit our special concern. Their eligibility is based on service to Canada during a time of war. These people, both servicemen and civilians, risked their lives for their country. We should not forget that they are entitled, not to favours, but to what they have so valiantly earned and justly deserved. The adoption of this bill will simply assure these people a better standard of living.
Many of these men left home and enlisted at an early age and, because of the years they spent in the service of their country, were not always able on their return to improve their education or training to attain a degree of skill which would have been within their reach had they not enlisted. The result is that in later years when they suffer some disability, which may not be directly caused by their war service, they have difficulty in providing for themselves and their families. These men are, to a large degree, casualties of war, although they may not have been wounded. Their widows and orphans also deserve our special consideration.
I believe, Sir, that the measures proposed in this bill will be welcomed by every member of this House as concrete evidence of our awareness of the special contribution this group of Canadian citizens has made to their country and as a clear indication of our commitment to treat them in a fair and just manner.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the past two months of tension in this House of Commons I think that during the debate on Bill C-148 you will see a change of tempo. There will be no banter back and forth across the floor. I can assure you that the Veterans Affairs Committee is a committee, the members of which have comradeship, esprit de corps and understanding. We are dealing with a topic that is diminishing in importance in the country. It is a topic which nobody can argue is anything but significant in our society, since it relates to the war veterans of Canada who deserve everything we can give them.
I am pleased to follow the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), who is presenting his first bill in the House of Commons, and I congratulate him. While I did congratulate him at the committee hearings when we were discussing the supplementary estimates, I hope members will allow me to repeat what I said as I feel it should be placed in the Hansard record. I repeat my

March 8, 1973
War Veterans Allowance Act congratulations because, as I said, the minister should be an example for all Canada, certainly to those of us here, of what a Canadian can accomplish against all odds and adversities suffered while defending his country. The minister came back to Canada and, as a double amputee, gained the highest achievement to which a veteran in this country of ours could aspire, becoming the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
I know, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the time to be handing out bouquets to members opposite or ministers, but perhaps it does not hurt once in a while to have the opportunity to exhibit a little human understanding and compassion.
I am pleased also that the introduction of this bill gives us an opportunity to discuss a topic which, as I said before, is unfortunately diminishing in importance in Canada. That topic is veterans affairs. It is diminishing in importance because people are preoccupied with beating each other's brains apart over the material things that seem to be so important. Even with all the expertise at our disposal, we cannot seem to solve the important problems. I am sure the minister knows what I mean, and I am sure he will agree that with all the unrest in the country, Canadian governments could look to the veterans organizations to get an example of comradeship, neighbourliness and humanity. In our continuous struggle to prevent a breakdown in national unity we try to legislate, set up studies and commissions or sit at conferences. I say, Mr. Speaker, that national unity cannot be legislated by governments, by sitting around a conference table, by studies and commissions or by presenting bills in parliament. National unity is created in the hearts of people and is passed on over the years because our ancestors suffered hardship in discovering and building Canada and in making it the great nation it is today.
The veterans of Canada protected the unity of our country in the First and Second World Wars, and in Korea, when they pledged their loyalty to Queen and country and defended Canada against tyranny. They went to foreign countries to do so as well as to protect other nations of the world because our country asked them to do so. They did not ask for any special favours. The contracts they signed were all one-sided. There were no fringe benefits, no automatic increases in pay and allowances, no hospital benefits. What is most important is that they fought together, not as citizens of different origins, not as English or French or any particular race, creed or colour. They fought together against a common enemy as Canadians.
Today, with all the expertise we have we are trying to find out why the youth of Canada are reacting against the establishment. We also hear frequently about their abhorrence of anything military and their attitude against war. I have no quarrel with their attitude. Nobody wants war. I apologize for saying that I have a son who also hates mention of the word "war". I do not want him or any of my children to ever experience war. But let me remind the youth of our country that there are thousands of graves over in Europe of young lads who were 18 and 19, yes, and

even younger, who did not like the word "war" in World Wars I and II. Some of them even lied about their ages so that they could come to the defence of their country, their parents or loved ones. They should be here now enjoying our prosperity and taking advantage of the supposed opportunities that exist; but they cannot because they lie in the war graves of Europe.
May I respectfully suggest to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) that in his youth exchange programs he might show a little patriotism by arranging some trips to the war graves of Europe if he wants to do something worthwhile for our youth and for the benefit of this country. We cannot blame our youth for the failure of our governments to live up to their commitments to our veterans for the past 50 years. Yes, we forget too easily, and perhaps I should put on the record these words which appear on one of the war graves in Europe:
Here we lie because we did not choose to live and shame the land from which we sprung. Life to be sure is nothing much to lose, but young men think it is . . . And we were young.
Those were the youths of past world wars; those were the youths who had the right to live, to react and to demonstrate. Perhaps some of them might even be sitting here as members of parliament today, but I am not sure how much they would appreciate what is happening. But we forget so easily. Nobody in his right mind wants a war. But we have to go to war because of the stupidity and selfishness of those who govern, and because of the greed, hate and ambition that lies in the twisted minds of those who gain power through deviousness and the quest for power.
We have seen examples in recent weeks of the results of the war in Viet Nam in which thousands of young Americans also lost their opportunity to enjoy the great future that they had hoped their country would provide. And what did our governments do during the past 54 years for those Canadians who went to three wars for the same reason? I cannot use more forceful words than the veterans organizations did which presented a brief to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs during the joint study on the basic rate of pension. They state:
The dollar value of war disability pensions for 100 per cent disability pensioners, has because of erosion and neglect fallen to a critical level.
This has happened because of the failure of successive governments in the last 50 years to maintain the basic rate of pension at approximately the same level as that paid to unskilled workers in the public service.
It is not 50 years but more like 54 years. There are almost one million war veterans in Canada today who served our country. Many thousands of them made their sacrifice but returned to Canada, took up their lives and occupations and became successful. They caught up to society because of their initiative, drive and knowledge. But they are still veterans. They maintain their interest in their fellow comrades and belong to veterans organizations with the sole purpose of helping their comrades. Some of the successful ones even sit here today as Members of Parliament trying to do their best for their country and for their comrades. But many came back maimed and disabled. They do not want to beg from government, but they are forced to do so because they lost the best years of their lives fighting for their country. The veterans we are
March 8, 1973

talking about are either too disabled to take their place in society or are those who fall into the category of the burnt-out pensioner.
This brings me to the subject of the bill before us, Bill C-148 to amend the War Veterans Allowances Act. I cannot personally, or on behalf of my party, quarrel with the amendments before us because they are good amendments. The bill provides for allowances to $151.14 for the single veteran and $257.21 for the married veteran with an allowable income of $40 and $70. There are supplementary benefits which one in the opposition should not mention, but I feel a most important amendment is the repeal of section 8 which removes the limitation in respect of payment of an allowance to a person who owns personal property. It also removes certain powers in relation to transfer of property in determining the amount of an allowance and provides for the future escalation of allowances under the act to commence on January 1, 1974. May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted at five o'clock I was giving kudos to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald). I wanted to mention the changes introduced by order in council rather than as amendments to the act. Some of these were as follows: First, the removal of the penalty imposed on recipients who own and occupy their own home valued in excess of $10,000; second, the removal of the penalties imposed on the sale of the home of the veteran; third, the increase by 25 per cent of the casual earnings of a veteran; fourth, the exemption of $15 and $30 for the veteran, either single or married, who qualifies for OAS/GIS.
I would like to say, with the utmost respect and sincerity, that this and past governments cannot be too proud of the fact that finally in 1973, some 54 years after the First World War, the war veterans allowance has reached a satisfactory figure. Some people may attack me for saying this because the war veterans allowance only came into effect in 1930, but we can take it all under the umbrella of the Pension Act. I can only repeat once more the words in the brief submitted by the war veterans' associations to the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs dealing with the joint study report on the basic rate of pension:
This has happened because of the failure of successive governments in the last 50 years to maintain the basic rate of pension at approximately the same level as that paid to unskilled workers in the public service.
The same can be said about war veterans allowances. Veterans are now in the twilight stages of their lives. The First World War veteran is in his late seventies and cannot take advantage of the increase permitted in casual earnings because he is long past the stage when he can work. The World War II veteran is now in his late fifties, and with our new thinking in society today he is long beyond the stage of consideration even for work on a LIP project. Probably the increase in casual earnings will help this veteran, the one whose children are grown up and educated, whose children have gone out on their own. He or his wife may earn a little more income to find a little extra comfort in their later years. Why couldn't the government give a little consideration to these people and increase the allowable earnings to something more meaningful, so that a veteran could enjoy some comfort and at the same time get back a feeling of contributing to society?
None of those who sat in government over the past 50 years can be proud. I do not blame the present minister; I

March 8, 1973

blame all past governments. Here again we have an opportunity to correct all the inequities in the War Veterans Allowance Act, and we still leave some items uncorrected. For example, under the War Veterans Allowance Act a widow or widower responsible for the support of a child may draw the married rate. However, this ceases when the child reaches 21 years of age. This is a great imposition if the child desires to continue in school. Surely we can amend the act to raise the age to 25, to give the child a better opportunity to complete his or her education.
Under the eligibility clause of non-resident recipients, war veterans allowance may be paid to an eligible person who absents himself from Canada if, on the day that he leaves Canada, he is a recipient of the allowance and was resident in Canada for 12 months immediately preceding that day. There are many Canadian veterans who elected to stay in the United Kingdom, however, Mr. Speaker, which should be their right, and because they elected to stay there they are discriminated against. In order to qualify, they would have to move back to Canada for 365 days. Would it be too much to expect our government to finally show some recognition of the contribution they made during the conflicts? Can we have a clear conscience by denying these Canadians, the few hundred of them, the benefit of war veterans allowance just because they decided to stay in a foreign country?
Also, what about the veteran who is in the category where he qualifies, because of the size of his family, under the Canada Assistance Plan and each increase in the war veterans allowance by the federal government is charged against the amount he is receiving on social assistance? Is it not reasonable to give this veteran the same exemption that the veteran gets if he falls into the old age security category? Is he not in the same need? The criteria for war veterans allowance, and specifically the clause covering exempt income, state that certain specified benefits such as attendance allowance, additional pension paid on behalf of children and social assistance paid on behalf of children, are not assessed as income, but some provinces do charge these increases against social assistance payments. Here is another clause which must be corrected before it is too late:
Under eligibility a veteran must have served at least 365 days in the United Kingdom during World War I and prior to November 12, 1918.
I have had cases come to me of veterans in this category having served 364 days, and the department will not allow some flexibility. Is it not long past the time when we should show some human consideration, which we preach to the rooftops at election time, so that he can enjoy the exemptions under old age security and have the right to treatment services?
I have no hesitation in congratulating the minister and the government for taking the steps necessary to introduce the amendments raising the war veterans allowance as indicated in the tables at the back of the bill. I give them full marks. But there is no reason whatsoever why we should not stop and think of our commitment to all the veterans of Canada expressed over 50 years ago. Unless we do it now, Mr. Speaker, while we have the opportunity
War Veterans Allowance Act
under Bill C-148, it should ever remain on the conscience of the government that we have failed in this commitment.
For the benefit of the veterans of Canada, we accept without question the amendments offered but we commit ourselves to the following further amendments: First, to repeal the age limit of orphans and increase the age of eligibility to 25 years; second, that we would immediately consult the provinces and provide the funds necessary to eliminate the restriction charging increases in war veterans allowances against veterans' social assistance benefits; third, that we would repeal the clause restricting the eligibility of World War I veterans to those having served 365 days in the United Kingdom; fourth, that we would repeal the clause making it obligatory for war veterans who elected to stay in foreign countries to reside in Canada for 365 days in order to qualify for the war veterans allowance; fifth, that we would raise the allowable casual earnings of war veterans receiving war veterans allowances to $1,200 for the single veteran and $2,000 for the married veteran.
The married veteran cannot take advantage anyway, because he would be 79 years old and cannot work. But let us give the World War II veterans and the Korean veterans the benefit of trying to get a little extra income for the comforts they deserve.
Under the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act we must seek out those who, although civilians, served in theatres of war and contributed to the war effort, because they too risked their lives on behalf of their country. I refer, Mr. Speaker, to the firefighters, the Newfoundland foresters, the auxiliary service workers, the merchant seamen, the salt water fishermen and all those others who had a part to play in conflicts against the enemy.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, because this bill restricts reference to disability pensioners I should like to mention the joint study report on the basic rate of pension and emphasize the co-operation of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. The joint study report, authorized by the former minister of veterans affairs and supported by the present minister, which came before the committee was accepted unanimously without even hearing all the witnesses who were supposed to appear. This study was carried out by a joint committee consisting of veterans' organizations and the Department of Veterans Affairs, and was chaired by the chairman of the Pension Commission.
The recommendations contained the following: that the basic rate of pension, after so many years of procrastination, for the single, 100 per cent pensioner be based on the average salary of the five lowest categories in the public service. This would increase the basic rate of pension from the present $3,793 to $4,529. Further, Mr. Speaker, in calculating increases in the wages of these public servants rather than on the cost of living index, so that finally we could establish an equitable consideration for the disabled war veteran. I was authorized, and stated on behalf of my party, that we would accept the recommendations without debate. This was authorized by my leader. The minister is in full agreement with this new formula, Mr. Speaker, and I only hope that the cabinet will produce

March 8, 1973
War Veterans Allowance Act
legislation to support these recommendations of the standing committee.
I have tried to be responsible tonight in my remarks to the government on the bill before us. We all know that the minister wants to do what is best for the war veterans of Canada. However, I warn the government that if we do not get the legislation produced following the recommendations of the joint study report, all-out war will be declared by my party.
Finally, in the interest of the war veterans of Canada, which interest is shared by my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), we are prepared to pass this stage of the bill, without further debate, at ten o'clock. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention three people who assisted the veterans affairs committee: the chairman of the War Veterans Allowance Board, who has over the years displayed the keenest interest in the future of the veterans who fall within the criteria of the War Veterans Allowances Act; the chairman of the Pension Commission, who since the implementation of the Woods committee report has been devoted to the cause of the veteran; and Mr. C. Chatterton, who served on the Woods committee and who since the war has devoted his life to the betterment of conditions for war amputees and all other Canadian veterans.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in spite of what goes on in this House, I should like to pay tribute to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who has devoted himself to the cause of the pensioner in whatever category.
