subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is for me a distinct honour to follow in this debate two such distinguished veterans as the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) and the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). Like them, I wish to express my very real pleasure in serving as a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs. As the previous speaker indicated earlier, it is not a committee like all the others. Like him, I also want to say that we welcome Bill C-148, which seeks to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act and in the process will make certain consequential changes in the administration of the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. We are quite happy that it has been possible to reach agreement for this bill to be given second reading not later than ten o'clock this evening so that it can be sent to the committee and put into legislation just as soon as possible.
[DOT] <2020)
Like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, I am aware of the other piece of legislation that we hope will be before the House before long, namely, a bill to amend the Pension Act implementing the recommendations made by the joint study group which considered the basic rate of the pension under that act. As I have already

had occasion to say, I regard that report, which our committee endorsed unanimously and with expedition, as containing some very important recommendations. To begin with, it solves the problem of what the basic rate of the 100 per cent disability pension should be. On the other hand, it proposes a formula for escalating that pension in future years which is the best and most progressive escalation formula that has ever been put on the table of this House of Commons. I hope that when the minister takes this matter to cabinet he will make sure that he gets that escalation formula into the bill along with the formula for determining the basic rate of the pension.
Tonight we are not dealing with the Pension Act-that will come later-but with this bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. I realize that both previous speakers made some reference to what it does. Perhaps I might be permitted, even at the risk of repetition, to indicate briefly the provisions of this amending bill as I see them. First, it raises the amount of the allowance that can be paid to a single veteran under the War Veterans Allowance Act from the present figure of $131 to $151.14. This increase combines two things, the cost of living escalation, in the allowance itself, that came into effect at the beginning of January, plus the amount by which the old age security is being increased, with the result that the total allowance paid to a single veteran is greater than it was previously by the addition of those two amounts.
In addition to raising the maximum allowance that can be paid from $131 to $151.14, and perhaps even more important, it raises the ceiling on the total income that is permissible to a single veteran from $171 to $191.14. Again, the amount of that difference, which is a total of $20.14, is a combination of the cost of living escalation in the war veterans allowance that took place in January, plus the $13.39 by which the old age security pension is being increased. Although it raises the ceiling from $171 to $191.14, I must point out that for single veterans over 65 it really raises the ceiling from $186 to $206.14, by virtue of the fact that the extra $15 that such veterans got in 1972 is not counted for purposes of the ceiling under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
In parallel terms, this bill raises the allowance that can be paid to a married veteran from $217.61, by a total of $39.60, arrived at in the same way, to a total of $257.21. Again, it raises the more important figure, namely, the ceiling on permissible income, from $287.61, again by $39.60, to $327.21. I must point out, however, that if that married veteran and his wife are both over 65, there is another $30 in the picture. The ceiling then goes up from what was a total of $317.61 to a new ceiling of $357.21.
There is something I want to say right away about this in complimentary terms. I am glad that on this occasion the government is not giving with one hand and taking away with the other. The veteran who is under the War Veterans Allowance Act gets the full benefit of the cost of living escalation that took place in January and the full benefit of the increase in old age security. It is not given here and taken off there. In a moment or two I shall be saying there are some things about which I am not satisfied, but I am glad that on at least that point we have not had to do any arguing at all. It is also good to get these
March 8, 1973

higher allowances and ceilings, but I still think they are not high enough.
There are some anomalies that have crept into this picture which I think are unacceptable. I feel very strongly that we must straighten them out. Some have been referred to by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's St. Barbe. I think that he and I and all members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs are agreed that the time has come for us to do a thorough overhaul of the War Veterans Allowance Act, just as in the past few years we did a thorough overhaul of the Pension Act.
One of the anomalies that is most unfortunate arises because the extra $15 to a single veteran, and the extra $30 to a married veteran, if he and his wife are over 65, that were allowed last year above the ceiling were allowed by virtue of an order in council that simply said those OAS-GIS increases did not count. The ceilings were not raised; they were left where they were, but there was a special provision that this extra OAS-GIS money granted in 1972 would not be counted under the ceiling. The result is that we have this strange picture. In the case of a single veteran over 65, his effective ceiling, the one that counts, is $206.14, but the single veteran under 65 has a ceiling on the total income he can have, if he is a war veterans allowance recipient, of $191.14. I think that is quite unfair.
Likewise, if you look at the case of married veteran you find this situation. If the married veteran is over 65 and his wife is also over 65, the effective ceiling for that veteran is $357.21. In the case of the married veteran where one is over 65 and the other is under 65, the effective ceiling is $342.21. To complete the picture, if a married veteran on the war veterans allowance and his wife are both under 65, the ceiling is $327.21.
Now, it did not start out in this way at all. The hon. member referred to the fact that this act came into being in 1930. Yes, it came in in the spring of 1930. I think I can say this, to demonstrate the non-partisan nature of our approach on the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs: it was introduced in the spring of 1930 when the government of Mackenzie King was in power, and first came into effect in the fall of 1930, when the government of R.B. Bennett was in power.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext: Were you here then, Stan?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
I was not here then, but I voted for the first time in the election of that year, and I voted for J.S. Woodsworth in Winnipeg North Centre.
I was speaking about the history of this act, which was first brought in in 1930. That was just three or four years after the old age pension of those days had come into effect. The first war veterans allowance was exactly like the first old age pension, except for the age at which benefits were available. The amount was exactly the same, $20 a month or $240 a year, with a ceiling on total income of $365 a year or about $30 per month. That ceiling applied to both pieces of legislation. The difference was that the veteran could get war veterans allowance at the age of 60, whereas the civilian could not get old age pension until he was 70. But there was no difference
War Veterans Allowance Act
between those veterans who were over or under 65. There was no provision saying that if you were 65 you would get a higher ceiling than if you were under 65.
I am sure no one intended this, but that is the way it has developed because of the anomalies which have crept into the picture. I urge strongly that this be corrected. It could be corrected very simply, by writing into the act new ceilings the equal of the highest effective ceilings that we now have, instead of allowing it to be done by order in council. We should not continue this kind of discrimination.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe referred to veterans who are on welfare programs and are getting money that comes eventually from the Canada Assistance Plan. This, of course, will involve people under 65. Although they get money from public funds in that way, there is a lower ceiling imposed on them when they are under 65 that does not apply to veterans who are over 65. I think this ought to be straightened out. Even though I am arguing that we should review the War Veterans Allowance Act in its entirety, I think this is something which we should try to correct at this time.
Another anomaly that has developed because of this legislation having been built up more or less as a piece of patchwork is this. As it now stands, a single veteran is entitled to a total of $206.14 if he is 65 years of age or over. But he already can get under the new old age security legislation, after it is passed, $170.14. This includes both OAS and GIS. That means that all the War Veterans Allowance Board will pay him is $36; yes, that is all. And if he has a small disability pension, it will cut that amount down. Mr. Speaker, $36 is the possible figure and there are many single veterans who will fit into that pattern. There are many single veterans over 65 who will get the old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement, amounting to $170.14, and they will get $36 in war veterans allowance, which will bring their total benefit to $206.14. On the other hand, if you look at the case of the married veteran where both he and his wife are over 65, you will find that the total they can get under the ceiling is $357.21. They will get $324.60 in OAS and GIS, which leaves the total that they can get as war veterans allowance of $32.61.
Let me compare the figures again, in case I have not made them clear. The single veteran over 65 will get $36 from the War Veterans Allowance Board, but the married veteran over 65 will get only $32.61. Not only does the married veteran not get twice as much as the single veteran gets; he gets $3.39 less than the single veteran. As I say, I know how this program has been built up and I know you must take the total picture into consideration, but I suggest that the practice that has developed is unfair. The more veterans find they are, as it were, taken away from special veterans legislation and handled under general pensions legislation or general welfare legislation, the more they feel that they are not being given the rights to which they are entitled as veterans. I urge very strongly that we try to correct that anomaly, preferably when we have the bill in committee but certainly by instituting a complete overhaul of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I now move to the question of the removal of property qualifications which have been included in the act, up to

March 8, 1973
War Veterans Allowance Act now, ever since it was passed in 1930. I welcome it most warmly and I congratulate the minister for bringing in this very significant and progressive change. When I think of all the widows over the years who, on becoming widows, sold the house and other assets and had to wait until they had used up the proceeds of that sale until their assets had been reduced to a certain figure, I wish we could make this provision retroactive; but I fear that far too many of them have gone to a place were we cannot send them any money.
The property qualification under the War Veterans Allowance Act was a disgrace and I am delighted that it is being removed. I understand that property and money in the bank will still be considered, in the sense that the interest on that money will count as income for the purposes of the means test in the act. However, at least doing away with the requirement to bring the value of property owned down to a certain figure is a progressive, humane step and I congratulate the minister on bringing in this provision tonight.
Like the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, I regret that nothing has yet been done about those Canadian veterans who could qualify under the War Veterans Allowance Act except for the fact that they reside in the United Kingdom or other countries in the world and, therefore, have not met all the requirements that are in this act. I was pleased to hear the deputy minister say in the committee the other day, when we were given a preview of this legislation, that overcoming this problem is not administratively difficult. We tried to put the pressure on the mandarins to solve the problem, and the mandarins suggested that this was a matter of policy and had to go to cabinet. At the moment the mandarins and members of cabinet are within reach of my voice. The chief mandarin of this department is up there in the gallery, listening, and the minister is in the House.
I hope this problem will not be passed back and forth much longer. It is administratively possible to correct this situation, said the deputy minister but he contended it was a matter of policy. I hope that this difficulty will be solved. I think it really is incredible that Canadian veterans who choose to remain in the United Kingdom are not able to get the benefit of this legislation.
One of the changes that was made a couple of years ago was the one that denies to the widow of a war veterans allowance recipient the full married rate for one year. This is something which ought to be looked at again. I think we ought to reinstate the original provision. I hope I have said enough to indicate that in my view, and in the view of the hon. member who spoke just before me, although there is nothing in this bill that is not good and although we welcome everything in it, what is wrong is that it is not good enough. We think that the anomalies to which I have referred should be straightened out and the act should be reviewed and greatly improved.
Both the previous speaker and I referred to this act as having come into being in 1930. I mentioned that it was first drafted just three or four years after the first old age pension bill was passed by parliament. I remind hon. members again of the similarities between the two pieces of legislation. They are almost identical except for the fact that the veteran could get his benefits at age 60 and the

civilian had to wait until he was 70. The other difference was that the old age pension was administered by the Department of Finance, and that kept the amount low enough, whereas the war veterans allowance was administered by the then department of pensions and national health. Otherwise, these laws were the same.
We have moved a long way in the field of pensions, a long way from the concept of a means test as it was applied to the old age pension of the late 1920s and early 1930s. I think we should get away from that concept completely as far as the War Veterans Allowance Act is concerned. In a decade when we are talking of new methods of income maintenance, when we are talking of a guaranteed income, I think the time has come to consider the veterans who served this country as the group for whom the concept of a guaranteed annual income should begin. I should like to see the War Veterans Allowance Act, an act that has served its purpose well during the last 40 years or more, turned into a guaranteed annual income for all veterans who reach a certain age, or all veterans of any age who need it because of poor health or other reasons and who cannot qualify for a pension under the Pension Act.
The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe referred to those veterans of the First World War of very advanced age now. When I hear of cases of veterans who are now 70 or 80 years of age still having difficulty trying to establish their claims-the new legislation permits veterans to reopen their cases now-it seems to me it would be much simpler to establish a category such that all veterans 75 years of age or over would receive a certain allowance on a guaranteed basis without any questions asked. But then let us bring that age down, yes to 50, for veterans of more recent wars, and guarantee to all of them the standard of living they deserve.
I have had a lot to say over the years that has been critical of the shortcomings in veterans legislation. I remember that when I first came here one of the things lacking in the War Veterans Allowance Act was any provision for widows. During World War II we finally got them covered, first of all by an item in the estimates, then after a while by order in council under the War Measures Act, and finally, some time after the end of World War II, we got the widows covered under the War Veterans Allowance Act itself.
It has been a good piece of legislation and we have made it better over the years. Many Canadian veterans have benefited under the War Veterans Allowance Act. But we are no longer in the 1920s or 1930s. We are no longer in the means test or welfare age; we are in an age where we talk of rights. If any persons in this country have a sacred right, it is the veterans who have served us, and their survivors. I think we should move as quickly as we can to transform the War Veterans Allowance Act into a guaranteed income act for all the veterans of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join the other speakers who took part in the debate on this bill concerning the condition of veterans.
March 8, 1973

Besides asking on their behalf for an increase in their pensions, we want to pay tribute today to those who fought for the greatest principles of civilization. It was to uphold all those great principles that our veterans fought. They are now fighting to obtain the right to live in a community whose wealth exceed the needs, even if those needs have not yet been fulfilled.
What we are asking is that this government increase the veterans pensions like the old age pension. Since we have raised pensions for a certain category of people, we must also raise those of veterans. Otherwise, it would be unfair, the administration would not be sound and we would ignore one class of citizens that should have priority because these people have dedicated themselves, suffered ill treatments and done some work that the others have not done.
But if we intend to increase these pensions, this country must be able to do so and we must analyze all sectors of society to find out whether it is truly possible.
We must also know what effect a pension increase can have on the population. Is it good to ir crease pensions? Is it good to increase this or that? Are we really in a position to do it? Will that restore the economic balance or make it worse?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to develop this subject because I think that all those increases are throwing the economy further out of kilter. I strongly believe that they are not the right solutions. I say right now that we are not against higher pensions for senior citizens or veterans because they have a right to those increases just as well as others. However I also say that those increases are not normal, because we only consider higher pensions without thinking about replenishing the source so that it does not run dry. We draw from that source as if it were endless, without caring about the necessary repairs to that source on which the population feeds itself.
So, if we want the population to go on living and progressing, the feeding sources must be abundant. We must work on them, dig through them and modify them until we find plenty of water to provide everything we need for the population. The only way we find at present is to increase pensions.
Industrialized countries have known a strong economic growth in 1972. As soon as confidence returned after the national economic crisis of August 1971, growth accelerated everywhere, in Europe, in Japan and in North America. In large industrialized countries, the rate of production almost doubled as compared with the previous year. In 1972, the gross national product went up from 10.5 to 11 per cent, per capita personal income increased by almost 10.5 per cent, while the standard of living of Canadians rose by only 5.5 per cent.
As shown in per capita consumer expenditures, national revenue increases, interest rates have gone up alarmingly and the income of financial institutions has reached unprecedented levels.
But middle businessmen's incomes have substantially decreased. The income of ordinary businessmen is reduced to almost nothing because the government must

grant pensions since some people live in shameful and abject poverty.
Mr. Speaker, we are still facing two major issues: unemployment and rising prices. We must unhappily admit that the level of unemployment is too high and that we must take steps to solve these problems. We must give stronger momentum to the economic growth and reduce unemployment. To correct this situation, we suggest boosting pensions in order to decrease unemployment.
I am still wondering, Mr. Speaker, whether we are really going in the right direction to reach our objective, namely to lower the level of unemployment by increasing pensions, while at the same time coping with the rise in the cost of living and prices. That was the casue of the economic unrest in 1972.
The increase in consumer prices specially affected food prices, which have spiraled. I shall not go into a long description of the reasons for increases. The present economic system is the direct cause of loss of purchasing power. Therefore, higher veterans allowances and pensions of other citizens are being called for.
As a result of pressure from the opposition, the government has decided to give priority to increasing veterans allowances' and old age pensions. Veterans' allowances will be upped to $151 a month for single beneficiaries or persons living alone and $257 for married couples. These increases, according to the minister's statement, would cost $9 million in 1973-74.
As for the veterans, the committee will say in its report what it recommends as an increase for their disability pensions. The committee is working on that problem and it is on those objectives that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) based his remarks a while ago proposing adjustments to give justice to all and provide a better balance between the incomes of married and single people.
In fact, veterans suffer like all others from the disastrous increases in the cost of living. Therefore, they are as entitled to increases in their pensions as others.
We still think that all those increases further unbalance our economy. Those monies could help reduce the cost of living by way of a compensated discount. Instead of raising pensions of all types, it would have been wiser to reduce the cost of living. Then all taxpayers would have benefited from it. The economy would have been stimulated in a general way and that would have allowed us to boost the purchasing power of people, to create jobs, to neutralize the economy and to do away with inflation while at the same time providing more tax relief for taxpayers.
We then come to realize that the economic balance can be restored and stabilized only by raising those pensions of all types. So we are for any logical increase, but we would like to have the most logical and practical system so as to be in a position to allow Canadians to live decently in their country which is not lacking in resources or production.
Nobody in this country worries about where he will find goods he needs. But all Canadians are concerned about tomorrow, they wonder where they will find the scraps of paper that they need to meet their needs. They do not

But there is only one way to have money: it is to borrow it and to pay interest. The governments are doing the same thing and it is impossible for them to further increase pensions because the cost of living goes up and the situation of all citizens, young and old, gets more and more difficult. They find themselves in a rather precarious position because the cost of living is rising. Mr. Speaker, all things must first go through the mind. One has to know that. If there is a table, it is because a man conceived that table and then made it according to his own idea, with the materials and tools available to him.
To do a thing well, Mr. Speaker, you must first think of it and I believe that all the increases that are granting now have not been given enough thought, have been planned to build a viable economy according to basic principles and real facts.
Mr. Speaker, to do something well you should first give some thought and then try to do it as well as you imagine it. A painter is seldom completely satisfied with his work. Why? Precisely because the painting does not give a true picture of what he sees in his mind. This is an example, but we also know, Mr. Speaker, that the clearer a picture in the mind, the easier it becomes to realize, to produce and to materialize.
It is not for nothing that it is said, Mr. Speaker, that ideas rule the world; nothing can become visible before it has been thought of first.
So, before existing in reality, man was first conceived in God's spirit as well as his way of living on earth, according to nature which comprises material, cultural and spiritual elements. If, in the devine spirit, man was created to live in society, this man, in order to live well in society must first of all have in his own mind the vision of a beautiful, well-ordered, dignified, efficient and progressive life in society if he wants to live for each individual and for mankind.
That is the meaning of a real mind; the clearer our conception of society and of mankind, the more beautiful and fruitful will be life in society for all whose life is within themselves, within the family and within society. Both the aged and veterans are a part of this society.
Such is the environment of man's life on earth, in any country, including Canada in 1973.
The past helps us to understand Canada's present situation, with its inflation, unemployment, and monetary, economic and political poverty. The political orientation of a government that has been elected by the people of a country is expressed in financial terms.
If one's mind is really well developed, it becomes an easy matter to foresee how to bring about an economic

balance on a national scale between the family and business incomes that make up the economic life of Canada in 1973.
How, Mr. Speaker, are we to rid ourselves of poverty, unemployment and inflation, and enable every individual to lead a happy personal family and social life, when our monetary, political and economic machinery is such as it is?
The existing political and economic machinery is not in tune with the facts. Our political economic is leading us on a suicide course. The people is committing suicide because of a poor economy that fails to take account of its realities.
Mr. Speaker, instead of guiding Canada, the governments have become tax collectors, and the largest portion of those taxes, the most sacred portion, which should go to helping the citizens of Canada, the old people, but which escapes any discussion, is precisely that which goes for interest charges on the public debt. Because of that, the public lives in want and the governments in bondage, all that is needed to bring wellbeing to every country, every home exists. That is why finance does not reflect economic realities.
The financial system wreaks injustice upon the old, the veterans, children and families. Those who advocate it, those who accept it are party to injustice, to social disorder and anarchy; they are responsible for taxes and surtaxes, responsible for public debts and therefore responsible for unnecessary fears and deprivations. They are party to the injustice from which a large number of Canadians suffer.
The tax system is the consequence of a financial system based on injustice. Our financial system is based on our banking system. The banks control our financial system. They issue the money we call credit, basing themselves on the real wealth. In this case, the wealth of the country belongs to the country, to all its citizens. There is individual and collective wealth.
Bankers are people like any other people. They are making themselves the bookkeepers of the country's money and now they claim they own that money. They appropriate credit and cancel it when they so decide. TTiey are the absolute owners of the flow of money as they take over the creating and the cancellation of money.
Mr. Speaker, we want the people and the veterans in particular to have as much money as possible. We want them all to be happy and I think we all agree on this. However, in our present economic situation we cannot afford this, because the higher the pensions for the benefit of the individual the more we are creating problems for the people as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that the agreement we just reached proves the unanimity of everyone here. This bill has the acceptance of everyone
War Veterans Allowance Act
and we are all very anxious to vote on it. I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on this bill, for a few reasons, mainly for reasons of solidarity and to obtain justice for our former comrades who served in the armed forces with so many of us in the House during the dark days in Europe.

I would like, Mr. Speaker, to endorse the comments of my colleagues the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when they recalled the participation of our fellow citizens to that conflict which lasted almost five years and in which such a great number of our fellow citizens bravely fought.
The hon. member for Humbert-St. George's-St. Barbe also recalled, the participation or contribution of the members of the armed forces to the national unity in Canada. I agree with him wholeheartedly when he recalls the strength of that feeling of solidarity, the polarization of a cause accepted by all young Canadians many of whom had left an interesting career, either as businessmen or as professionals, either higher studies or a wife and a family.
So, for all these former comrades in the armed forces, Mr. Speaker, I think that we are all anxious to see to it that that legislation is enacted as soon as possible. [English]
I think that at this time it is appropriate that we should review briefly the origins of the War Veterans Allowance Act and restate the principles upon which it is based. I did some research on my own into this aspect of the legislation and I would like to share some of my findings with the House.
Many people are of the view that the War Veterans Allowance Act is the product of the depression years between World War I and World War II. This is not so, although the benefits proved to be of great assistance during those years. As a matter of fact, the problem of the burnt out veteran was under study in the early 1920s, several years before the depression. The problem had been recognized as early as 1922, and in 1928 and again in 1930 it was studied in detail by the special committee of parliament on pensions and returned soldiers' problems. When appearing before that committee on April 9, 1930, a spokesman for the minister of the then department of pensions and national health stated:
There are certain individuals at the present time, under the present pension act, who come to the department for assistance and help. These men are what have been called burnt out men; men of low pensions, and men who are no longer employable. If they went up for pension examination, the things from which they are suffering are of an intangible character; they are simply unable to work, and that before their time ...
It is something similar to what we see in using machinery. I might take as an example the locomotive that is geared up to drag a train along at 50 miles an hour, ordinary time, and some day the train is late and has to go 60 miles an hour to make up its time. When the end of that trip is reached, the coalbox is empty and the engine blowing off in all directions, while the engineer and fireman are worn out. It is that extra ten miles that has caused it.. .
We take the soldier who was overseas, and who was in the war front, he went under a driving that is much greater than probably most of us can conceive or realize-mental stress, and physical stress-and the mental stress was a considerable one . ..

March 8, 1973
War Veterans Allowance Act
We felt it was a pressure that others do not undergo. It was a wonder to us how the men in the front line stood what they did and for so long, so that this is advanced as a reason why consideration should be given to those men along this particular line ...
We know that they have the greatest difficulty in finding employment.
It is also interesting to note that when the original War Veterans Allowance Act was introduced in 1930, Bill-19, its preamble expressed the problem in these words:
Whereas there are a great number of veterans in Canada who are not in receipt of pensions under the provisions of the Pension Act...
And it is found that many pensioners and non-pensioners are, in fact, unemployable by reason of intangible results of their war service, apart from any consideration of pensionable disability; and it is desirable to provide assistance, or additional assistance, for these veterans in recognition of their service.
That expresses, I believe, quite clearly the reason for war veterans allowance. It was to make provision for men who were prematurely aged because of their war service. Because these conditions also apply to the veterans of other conflicts in which Canada has been involved, the benefits of the act have been extended from time to time so that veterans of the Northwest Field Force, the South African war, World War II and the Korean operation are now eligible. Coverage has also been extended to include the widows and orphans of such veterans.
There has been definite progress in this legislation through the years and no less than 15 changes have taken place since its inception in 1930. The original rate was $20 for a single veteran and $40 for a married veteran. Bill C-148 will once again update this important piece of legislation. It will provide for monthly payments, to those who qualify, of $151.14 for single veterans and $257.21 for married veterans. It will also remove the restrictions on personal property which have existed at various levels since the act was first passed.
This bill not only provides for the largest single increase in war veterans allowances in recent years, but also changes the character of the legislation and makes it a modified income-tested program. The men and women who will benefit from this bill are deserving of these changes. Many times we have said that they were the finest. I am proud to have been associated with this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am proud to speak in support of Bill C-148, an act to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am also proud to associate myself with those who have presented the bill and those who have worked so diligently and with such great compassion in preparing the studies and statistics required so that their thoughts could be translated into legislation. I believe we should also pay tribute to those persons who originated the study and to those who gave those conducting it the terms of reference necessary to prepare the supporting details for this bill.
Previous supporters of this bill have set down the changes and have commented on the increases in benefits that will accrue to the war veterans as the result of its passage. They have also pointed out some of the weaknesses that need looking into. I feel that they have been adequately covered and I do not intend to repeat those details. I just want to say a few words about veterans in general. War is a terrible act. The effects of war and the

after effects of war are equally terrible. Some people involved in the world wars and in the Korean war were able to find their way back into the mainstream of life. Some took a long time to rehabilitate, and some can never be rehabilitated. It is for the latter group that we are passing this legislation.
I am a war veteran and I am proud of whatever contribution I may have made. I was one of the lucky ones who were able to pick up the threads of life and continue on. But I left many friends in Europe, in the Middle East and in the Far East, young people full of hope and purpose who gave of themselves that others might live a full life. Some of my comrades and friends came home broken of body or mind, or both, and some came home with clouds in their minds because of suffering they had endured in prison camps or from grievous field wounds. They had left home light of spirit and with a purpose. Many did not not understand the full implications of war, but they readily accepted their responsibility and gave unselfishly of themselves in a just cause. I wish that today we could recapture some of that purpose. I wish we could catch the spirit and comradeship of those years, because then we could move mountains and overcome any obstacle in our path.
Each year when we have our Remembrance Day ceremonies I catch a glimpse of that spirit. I see the veterans line up to parade to the cenotaph. For a few fleeting moments their backs straighten, their heads take on a more jaunty angle and their eyes have that clarity of purpose reserved only for those persons who have seen war and who have returned. They remember because they can never forget. To many of them the war was a beginning, and unfortunately to some it was an end. But it is for those persons who fall between those two points that we bring forth Bill C-148 to help them in the later years of their lives. I hope the minister will be able to convince the cabinet to present a bill that will put into motion a legislative function that will ensure that they keep pace with a reasonable standard of living. I think all the members on the veterans affairs committee hope that this will happen. For many veterans this bill will be a new lease on life. It will allow them again to have some dignity and purpose. It will show them that we remember.
From all walks of life and from all professions, veterans left their homes and families to accept a challenge to the principles they had grown to accept as commonplace. Men and women undertook challenges that under normal circumstances perhaps would have frightened them. But they had that spirit and purpose which are so elusive today and are so needed.
I can only say, Mr. Speaker, that I am proud to associate myself with Bill C-148, an act to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am proud to associate myself with hon. members on all sides of the House who support this bill. I am proud to join hon. members who preceded me in lauding the efforts of those who drafted this bill and who did the preceding studies. I wish the bill God speed so that the recipients of war veterans allowance may receive the benefits contained in the bill at the earliest possible moment.
March 8, 1973

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-148, an act to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act, is one which I am very pleased to see before the House today. As a member who was fortunate enough to train here in Ottawa early in the war, I had in those days as a confrere the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). Those were in the days when we were on the same side.
When the War Veterans Allowance Act was first introduced, Canadian veterans, and British veterans domiciled in Canada at the date of their enlistment, with service in an actual theatre of war and disability pensioners were eligible for the allowance. Since then the act has been broadened to include widows of such veterans, orphans, dual service veterans and veterans who served during World War I in the United Kingdom for 365 days prior to the armistice. The act was also amended to include veterans of British Commonwealth and allied forces who were not domiciled in Canada at the date of their enlistment but had resided in Canada for ten years at the time of their application.
In order to receive the allowance outside of Canada, a person must have been a recipient at the time of his departure and must have resided in Canada for the 12 months immediately preceding the day he left Canada. The number of war veterans allowance recipients on March 31, 1972, was a little more than 75,000, of whom some 38,000 were from World War I and some 35,000 from World War II. The expenditure for the year amounted to some $73 million. It is interesting to note that five years ago there were over 86,000 recipients and the total expenditure was over $101 million. The administration of the War Veterans Allowance Act is the responsibility of the War Veterans Allowance Board. This board is a quasijudicial body, independent as far as its decisions are concerned, and acts as a court of appeal for applicants and recipients who are aggrieved by any decision of a district authority.
I appreciate the great value to war veterans allowance and to civilian war allowance recipients of the increases in the rates by $20.14 for single persons and $39.60 for those who are married. I realize that this will give over 100,000 Canadians increased purchasing power and therefore a justly deserved improvement in their standard of living. However, I would like to dwell briefly on the other main aspect of Bill C-148, the abolition of the personal property restriction. I realize that on November 9, 1972, the regulation imposing an assessment as income when the value of the recipient's home exceeded $10,000 was rescinded. This was a welcome step. However, the problem of personal property still remained. I am sure that many members of the House have received letters from constituents who have lamented the fact that they had slightly more in the way of personal property than the $1,250 single, or $2,5C0 if married, permitted by the act.
Some of these people knew that they could never again increase their personal property holdings, yet they realized they could not qualify for the allowance until they had expended their small surplus. Bill C-148, I am glad to say, will remove that problem. When this bill is passed, the value of personal property will no longer be a bar to eligibility. The tests for eligibility will be service and income.
War Veterans Allowance Act
I firmly believe that the citizens of Canada expect us to recognize with justice the sacrifices made for our freedom by this particular group of Canadians for whom the war veterans allowance was designed. I further believe that they will welcome this action on the part of the government and of parliament as a clear indication that it is our intention to continue to improve the legislation that affects this important segment of the Canadian public.
The record of the government in the field of veterans legislation is one with which I am honoured to be associated. I am proud of the record of Canada's serving men and women in two world wars and the Korean conflict, and I am proud of the measures that this government has taken and is taking to provide just recognition of their service and contribution to the cause of freedom.
The minister has dealt in detail with the other changes which have been made in the War Veterans Allowance Act and regulations. This bill is in keeping with the government's policy of improving veterans legislation so as to provide greater benefits to those who qualify. Mr. Speaker, I would also like to stress that in my opinion the changes which have taken place in the act and regulations in recent months, and the changes proposed in this bill, are important not only because they will increase the number of dollars in the pockets of the recipients, but also because they show a definite trend toward an increased recognition of the right of privacy of the individual. We will no longer be asking an applicant or recipient, "How much is your home worth?" We will no longer be asking him, "How much money do you have in the bank?" We will only be asking him to declare his income, and that, in my opinion, is a very reasonable request when the object of the legislation is to ensure that his income does not fall below the amounts provided by the act.
I sincerely believe that many of the recipients and many of those who will apply in the future will be happy to know that this step has been taken in order to respect their dignity and personal privacy. Mr. Speaker, this bill contains sound proposals and I heartily endorse it.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-148 has certain application to veterans of World War I who are the beneficiaries of increases in the payments under the act, and also with regard to the value of their holdings. For many years we have felt uncomfortable about the limitations imposed upon them and their spouses in regard to whatever property they may have accumulated during their lifetime. On the other hand, the casual benefits will be of little help because they are now of an age when it is rare that they are earning an income or have additional income that would be caught by the act. With regard to World War II veterans, however, these features are more important to them than they are to the first group. The World War II group will benefit by an increase in the payment which is commensurate with the increase in the old age security and the adjustment in the cost of living formula.
There is one thing that I have been hammering at. I would not draw attention to any individuals in this House within the sound of my voice, but they will know what I mean and it will be seen by anyone who cares to read the
25789-51 h

March 8, 1973
War Veterans Allowance Act proceedings of the veterans affairs committee in years past. It is what I consider the irrational, unrealistic and totally inequitable limitation on the payment of war veterans allowance to people who do not have the 365 days residence in Canada required for qualification.
At the committee meetings last June we had very serious discussions with the minister's officials and a study was promised. That was progress, because in the past the minister's predecessors had rejected my representations out of hand. Those conditions have not changed, Mr. Speaker. I would say to the minister that this is one area in which I thoroughly support my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) namely, the war veterans allowance should be paid to Canadian veterans who now live in Great Britain and Europe and have not qualified, by reason of the requirement of residence in Canada, since the end of hostilities.
We are told that there are administrative difficulties to bar the payments. I commend to the minister the representations put forward by the veterans' association in the United Kingdom. Year by year they have bombarded the ministry with their pleas. I know the people who administer the war veterans act in the United Kingdom, and there is not one word of truth or fact in the claim that there are administrative difficulties with regard to the men who do not have 365 days residence in Canada. The administration would be the same, and the number is small.
Mr. Speaker, we have veterans of World War I and World War II living in the United Kingdom under the conditions which are a downright shame. They are Canadians, and we maintain them over there in a condition of proud but undeniable poverty because of the inflexible attitude of the government on this rule. I for one who was a member of the Canadian armed forces during World War II absolutely refuse to accept this as a continuing condition and I hope that hon. members of this House will join with me in that crusade. This is not something that we must accept, any more than we can accept the conditions of prisoners of war.
If the minister and the government have seen fit to increase the ceiling with regard to the value of property under the War Veterans Allowance Act, what logical or equitable reason is there for maintaining an unrealistic ceiling under the Veterans Land Act? The action on property evaluations, mortgage ceilings and all the other matters were steps in the right direction. The minister was a good soldier during the war, but I must tell him that when you put one foot forward, you follow it with another and you go forward and make progress.
Mr. Speaker, I commend the government for this step forward with Bill C-148 and I urge, with all the sincerity that I as one of the veterans in this House can possibly bring forward, that they listen to the pleas of my colleagues on this side and members on the other side for justice for our veterans. Let us do them justice in today's circumstances, and not within the limits of the late 1940s and the 1950s with artificial ceilings which are totally unrealistic and unjust.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud to support the bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. [English.]
Mr. Speaker, this bill continues the fine tradition of this House in recognizing that Canada owes a special debt to the men and women who served our cause in time of war. These are the men who, because of their belief in our way of life, for $1.10 a day withstood the murderous gas attack at Saint Julian when troops of other countries could not stand, who took Vimy Ridge after other nations soldiers had failed, who fought gallantly at Beaumont-Hamel, Passchendaele, Cambrai and many other places.
These are the men who, paid $1.30 a day, landed in Sicily, defeated the enemy at Ortona, broke the Hitler line, assaulted the beaches of Dieppe, advanced the farthest of any allied troops on D-Day in 1944, liberated Holland and fought their way into the enemy heartland. They are the men who rolled and tossed in the destroyers and frigates of the North Atlantic convoys, and who faced the rigours of the aid to Russia sea route; others held steady in the flak of the bomber runs and maintained air umbrellas over the fighting troops.
The recipients of civilian war allowances include many of the merchant seamen who braved the cold, bleak, dangerous seas of the Murmansk run to deliver supplies to the Russians, or travelled on the Atlantic convoys taking supplies to beleaguered Britain. Their pay was small, their living conditions rigorous, and many were torpedoed and suffered hours in the chill Atlantic waters.
Bill C-148 will provide for an improved standard of living by increasing the rates and ceilings by $20.14 for single persons and $39.60 for those who are married. This will mean that the new monthly rates will be $151.14 single, $257.21 married, and the new annual income ceilings will be $2,293.68 single and $3,926.52 married. In addition, those who are in receipt of old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement will continue to benefit by an additional $15 a month single, and $30 married, by way of the exemption of those amounts of old age security pension and guaranteed income supplement.
Clause 2, which removes the limitations on personal property, is also of great importance because it will relieve many recipients of the disappointment and frustration experienced when from some source a small amount of personal property is acquired and as a result their allowance has to be cancelled and often an overpayment established. This clause will add to the peace of mind of many of the more than 78,000 recipients, and will also pave the way for others who are just over the personal property limitation to apply and qualify for the war veterans allowance or civilian war allowance.
This legislation is definitely in keeping with the attitude demonstrated by this government in earlier measures introduced and referred to by the minister which have improved the lot of war veterans allowance and civilian war allowance recipients. This government's pride in the accomplishment of Canada's servicemen and women is reflected in the measures by which we have provided for them. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Veterans

Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) for his ability, efficiency and a job well done, benefiting our veterans.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join in this debate on Bill C-148 and the amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Civilian War Pensions and Allowances Act. I join the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) in congratulating the minister on presenting this bill. This is the first bill he has presented to the House, although he appeared before the standing committee with regard to the study of basic rates which was carried out last year by the veterans' association and officials of the department. I must say that the minister acquitted himself very well before the committee. I am happy to join other hon. members in congratulating the minister in presenting his first bill to the House.
This bill will increase benefits allowed under the War Veterans Allowance Act as well as the ceiling on earnings of recipients. One important aspect of the bill is that it removes the limit on personal assets which a recipient may have at the time of making application. I understand this is called a modified income-tested program.
Last week we debated the Old Age Security Act and guaranteed income supplement bill. It is fitting that this is being followed by amendments increasing allowances under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Perhaps it is a tribute to the minister that he assumed his responsibilities at the time amendments were being brought forward to the Old Age Security Act with compatible increases being brought in at the same time to the war veterans allowance legislation. This bill is important to some 76,000 Canadians who are recipients of the war veterans allowance.
I wish to speak for a moment about the committee's study of basic rates, because I feel sure that in the not too distant future there will be pressure for the principle that was adopted by the committee to apply this to the War Veterans Allowance Act and other old age pension legislation. The principle is that we not only increase pensions annually by the amount of the cost of living, but by the increase in the standard of living. When the committee adopted the recommendations of this basic study report and recommended them to the House for acceptance, it was a very significant, almost revolutionary step because it has important implications for our whole old age security system.
Last year we tied the old age pension and veterans benefits to the cost of living index and the increases that take place there. In the past several years these have been in the order of 3 per cent or 4 per cent. I believe in 1972 it was 3.6 per cent and in 1973 it will be 4.5 per cent. This is not nearly keeping pace with the average increase in earning of Canadians, which is often in the realm of 6, 7 or 8 per cent. When we tie the benefits of the old age pension to the standard of living rather than the cost of living, there is a significant difference. It means that every so many years we do not have to go back and increase the basic amount in order to catch up with what has been lost due to the difference between the cost of living increase and the standard of living increase.
War Veterans Allowance Act
Mr. Speaker, I support Bill C-148. Perhaps by some standards it is a modest increase, but to the recipients of these benefits it is very important and significant.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words in support of this bill. As usually happens when veterans affairs legislation is before the House, there is complete unanimity of opinion. I echo the sentiments expressed by other members of my party, indeed, by members of all parties, in support of the bill now before the House.
I wish to pay special tribute to the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) on this, his first bill. It may not be customary for members of the opposition to pay tributes to the government, but on this occasion they are justly earned. I know that veterans throughout this country respect the new minister, not only because he is a veteran but also he is a veteran who has suffered, being a double amputee. That is a handicap which better enables him to judge the condition in which many veterans across this land find themselves.
Although it is impossible to turn back progress, if one can call it that, or change certain aspects of veterans legislation, I wish to protest the fact that the war veterans allowance is now to be mixed up with the old age pension and guaranteed income supplement. Many veterans consider the war veterans allowance as a burned out pension, if one may call it that. They fell that this pension is given to them because of the service they rendered to their country.
Many members of the House have paid tribute to our veterans. It seems to me that we are doing them a dishonour, if one may call it that, by mixing up payments under the war veterans allowance with payments under other social programs. As I have said, veterans feel that the allowance is theirs as of right because they served their country in time of need. Also, the pension and supplement are subject to income tax, whereas the war veterans allowance is exempt from such tax.
The big thing we must remember is the pride which veterans feel for having served their country. They feel that that service was recognized by the payment of what they call the burned out pension and what we call the war veterans allowance. I suppose there is no way to change this part of the legislation, but I think the Department of Veterans Affairs ought to take cognizance of what I have said. If it is possible on a future occasion to again give the veteran his just dues in the form of veterans allowance rather than in the form of pension, I think we should do so.
Apart from the increased benefits under this legislation, which are important, one of the most important parts of it is that which removes the restriction regarding the amount of property that a veteran may own before he is eligible for the full war veterans allowance. This new provision will certainly remove some of the roadblocks which have prevented veterans from receiving the full allowance. It is high time that this change was made. Veterans have protested to me, and I am sure to other hon. members, about the restriction on the amount they

March 8, 1973
Adjournment Debate
can earn. Granted, the ceiling has been raised. That is good and I do not quarrel with it. I ask, would we lose too much if we removed the ceiling altogether on veterans' earnings? Surely a veteran is making a contribution to society by the work he does, and we are doing him a great disservice by placing any ceiling on the amount he may earn and reducing his war veterans allowance accordingly.
Those are just a few of my thoughts, Mr. Speaker. Let me return to the war veterans allowance, or to the burned out pension as the veteran calls it. He has a certain pride in having served his country. I submit the allowance should be paid to him without any strings attached and without any liability for income tax. I will certainly support this bill, as will members on all sides of the House. I think the haste with which the bill was dealt with by the study group is evidence of the interest in it. We are ready to pass it almost immediately.
When this bill goes to committee I am sure we shall witness the same speedy consideration that the report of the study group received. I look forward to seeing the bill in committee very shortly so that we may work on it, bring it back to the House for final approval and make available to veterans benefits which will accrue from April 1.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-ADVANCE BOOKING CHARTER REGULATIONS-ASSURANCE THAT TRAVELLERS WILL BE PROTECTED AGAINST PRICE FIXING
AIR TRANSPORT-ADVANCE BOOKING CHARTER REGULATIONS-ASSURANCE THAT TRAVELLERS WILL BE PROTECTED AGAINST PRICE FIXING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes available to me this evening I hope the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay) will be in a position to clear up the confusion on questionable features surrounding the new regulations that were announced in January concerning advance booking charter regulations. For some time now a number of hon. members have been asking the minister questions in the House about the many areas of confusion and uncertainty surrounding the new regulations. I hope that after almost two months of concern, there will be some clarification of the regulations.
I know that the minister's powers are limited. The National Transportation Act limits the powers of the minister to alter decisions of the Canadian Transport Commission. However, the minister has responsibility for dealing with matters of transportation policy that affect our nation. Surely he is in a position to wield a great deal of influence in policy matters and in the bringing in of regulations that are prescribed by the Canadian Transport Commission within the ambit of the National Transportation Act. I say this in view of the many regulations which affect detrimentally many members of the travelling public. I believe it is fair to say that the regulations prescribed by the Canadian Transport Commission do not reflect the wishes of the travelling public nor the wishes of the retail travel trade.
In my opinion, without doubt the new regulations are making air charter travel more difficult. The new regulations are making air charter travel more confusing and more expensive. Above all, the new charter regulations do not provide the necessary protection against the so-called "bucket shop operator" or the undesirable operator who has plagued the charter industry in the past few years. Furthermore, it will place an increased burden on prospective charter passengers and also create undue hardship on the legitimate charter organizations who are dedicated to providing air charter travel to the many Canadians who are desirous of obtaining economic holiday travel.
I believe it is fair to say that these regulations are weighted very heavily in favour of the profitablity of the scheduled air services in this country at the expense of the travelling public. A look at the policy of price fixing, which in my opinion is monopolistic, reveals that foreign carriers are not allowed to file a tariff of fares that is below the fares filed by a Canadian carrier. As a result, undoubtedly air fares will be forced up to a much higher level.
The 90-day pre-booking requirement with a 25 per cent, non-refundable deposit places a very severe economic burden on those who are contemplating such holiday travel. In the event that a person has to change his holiday plans at the last minute, he has to surrender the 25 per cent deposit that he places on his trip. I seriously believe that this requirement should be altered and that there should be a 45 or 60-day pre-booking period. This has
March 8, 1973

been the suggestion made by a pioneer of the air charter industry in Canada, namely, Max Ward. I also believe that a great deal more flexibility should be given to the substitution of passengers using, say, a 30-day or perhaps 15-day period.
The whole matter of marketing the new ABC's has created a great deal of confusion and uncertainty. There has been delay in publishing the regulations. There has been delay in interpretation, which has created mass chaos in the air charter industry. We now have subsidiaries of airlines that are retailing the air charter bookings. We have Intervac, which is associated with Ward-Air, and Econair, associated with Air Canada, and so on. There is no question in my mind that these firms are operating at arm's length with the air lines.
I reiterate that the rules contained in the new regulations do not prevent the illegitimate operator from taking advantage of the public. I submit that the regulations should be tightened up. I believe they can be tightened up through meaningful discussion and consultation with the retail travel trade and with those engaged in the travel business. I must say that the whole approach to the formulation of these regulations was conducted on a unilateral basis. I believe the Canadian Transport Commission, in its wisdom, should have consulted to a much greater degree those involved in the travel business. Above all, we must know who is authorized and who is not authorized to organize a charter.
As reported at page 1758 of Hansard for February 28, the minister indicated that under section 43:37 of the regulations, permission may be authorized to depart from any of the provisions of the regulations, and I believe that this is welcome. Surely there is ample justification for this. Following a number of representations by interested travel groups, and indeed by myself, the minister recognized that there were indeed some very severe shortcomings and failings in the regulations.
I would urge the parliamentary secretary to consult his minister and members of the Canadian Transport Commission, persuading them to take due consideration of some of the further shortcomings I have enunciated this evening and, if necessary, scrap the regulations now prescribed because I believe they are unworkable. I think consideration should also be given to the fact that it is about time we recognized that the Canadian Transport Commission should concern itself more with the welfare of the travelling public than with the airlines and the railways to the degree it has in the past.
We are all aware of the lessons of the rail passenger service as a result of the protective shield provided by the Canadian Transport Commission. I urge that we do not allow that commission to shield the operations of the Airlines in the way it has shielded the operations of rail passenger services.

subtopic: CANADIAN CULTURE-MULTICULTURALISM-REQUEST FOR GRANT TO SASKATCHEWAN PROVINCIAL LIBRARY TO BUY BOOKS IN VARIOUS LANGUAGES
CANADIAN CULTURE-MULTICULTURALISM-REQUEST FOR GRANT TO SASKATCHEWAN PROVINCIAL LIBRARY TO BUY BOOKS IN VARIOUS LANGUAGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, March 6, I asked a question of the minister responsible for multiculturalism regarding library grants to the provincial library of Saskatchewan. The question was taken as notice by the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). I was disappointed that the minister responsible did not answer. However, I should like to outline in a little more detail the problem we have in this regard.
This problem has been brought to my attention by a number of letters from my own province. The provincial library in Saskatchewan has been carrying the operations of the public library system in that province and has from time to time provided multicultural services. In Saskatchewan we have small libraries and a regional library system which are financed largely by provincial government grants and also by local taxation.
Originally the service was adequate for the limited use to which it was put by a few borrowers. Gradually over the years the borrowers from that library have demanded improved library service in the many languages of the Saskatchewan pioneers. With increased attention to the question of bilingualism and multiculturalism in Canada, this will become more important to the people of Saskatchewan as time goes on. I should like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the reports of the 1971 census regarding the mother tongue of the population of Saskatchewan showed that 208,000 people, from a total population of 926,000, spoke neither English nor French as their first language. A total of 31,000 people in Saskatchewan spoke French as their first language. The breakdown by ethnic origin is still available only from the 1961 census. At that

March 8, 1973
Adjournment Debate
time, 550,000 out of 925,000 people were of non-British origin, and of these 60,000 were French.
For several years the provincial library has been buying books in the languages of the major ethnic groups. The budget for this program has always been extremely limited, and since the French language is placed in this group the collection is still extremely small. The original method of circulation was by sending blocks of 15 books in a language to the public library in the small towns of Saskatchewan. As the regional library system has been rapidly developing, the number of libraries has also greatly increased. People in charge of the various libraries have tried to increase the number of selections of books for an individual by increasing the number of blocks in a branch library. There has been an increase in the budget but it is not great enough to serve the people properly. So far, in this library books are available in the following languages: French, German, Ukrainian, Russian, Polish, Hungarian, Dutch, Czech and Slovak. There are still some demands which have not even been attempted to be met, for example, in the Swedish, Icelandic, Chinese and Italian languages, and so on.
They have also a fairly adequate collection of all types of material concerning the native Indians and the dialects of Saskatchewan. Last year, when an amount of $1 million was available through the Department of the Secretary of State, an attempt was made to obtain a grant to purchase more books for this library. This attempt was met with a roundabout "No". Members of the public service attempted to explain the impossibility of the federal government making a grant to a provincial government agency.
I should like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Saskatchewan co-operated wholeheartedly- and we agree with this-with the bilingual program. Many schools in my native province have started teaching French from grade one up. Of course, this program has been given an incentive through the grants obtained from the provincial government which originally come from the federal government. So there was no problem in obtaining grants for expanding bilingualism in the province of Saskatchewan. In the same way, the people of my province feel there should be no problem in obtaining a federal grant for a government agency in Saskatchewan to expand multiculturalism in that province, and indeed perhaps in any part of Canada.
Saskatchewan at present is also considering the use of the Cree and Chipewayen languages, in the northern areas of the province, in the school system. They are experimenting with many exciting ideas on multiculturalism. I feel that the answer I received on Tuesday was not adequate enough and I would like a more detailed statement from the minister or the parliamentary secretary.
