As a member from Quebec, I am extremely happy about that; I encourage him to go on in that direction and I can assure him that, as a French-speaking Canadian, I will always gladly co-operate with him in order that the formula which we have adopted concerning bilingualism and multiculturalism be complied with in co-operation with all citizens, whatsoever their ethnic origin.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-PROPOSED NEW RUNWAY-REQUEST FOR INFORMATION ON ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT
AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-PROPOSED NEW RUNWAY-REQUEST FOR INFORMATION ON ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, looking back over the last several months of debate which has taken place in the House concerning the proposed runway at Vancouver airport, I find we have a situation which I am certain has caused a great deal of anguish to members on this side of the House and also, I suspect, to some members on the government side.
Despite the fact that no adequate environmental studies have been made with respect to the possible or potential environmental damage caused by this new runway, the government has seen fit to proceed with the expropriation of the last of the homes in the affected area. As I said on another occasion in the House, in fact on several occasions, this is not the right way to make our decisions; this is not good environmental decision-making. If the truth were to be stated, I am probably supported by most members of the House when I say that the environmental impact must come at the front end of decision-making.
In answer to some questions raised in the House, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) said on February 15 this year, with respect to this new runway, as recorded at page 1335 of Hansard:
When we come to the expansion of the airport which will begin, say, in 18 months' time, we will need prior to that date a published environmental impact statement. I hope it can be prepared within 12 months; that is the deadline the task force is working to. It must gather all the information available to date. After the publication of that information we must hold hearings.
But it is curious that when this matter was raised on January 31 of this year, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) said, as recorded at page 829 of Hansard:
We have consulted all specialized government services on the consequences of noise and temperature on the environment. The Department of the Environment is supposed to collate all those reports. I shall be happy to send one to my hon. friend.
Mr. Speaker, the fact of the matter is that if the Minister of Transport was right on January 31, 1973, then the
March 8, 1973

Minister of the Environment did not need to make the statement that he made on February 15, 1973. And if you look through Hansard at the confusing replies coming from the government side, the only conclusion you can come to is that no environmental study was done and the government at the present time does not know what the environmental impact will be. But the Minister of the Environment has committed us to a 12-month deadline by which this study will be completed. To corroborate this, Mr. Speaker, on March 2, 1973, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) made a statement in the House of Commons, in the course of which he said:
-the Minister of the Environment will conduct a thorough study during the next 12 months into the effects of a new runway on the environment.
I draw to the attention of all hon. members and excerpt from a brief from the Vancouver Citizens' Committee for Noise Control, dated February 27, 1973. I quote only one short part of it. This refers to the amount of land fill that will take place at the mouth of the Fraser River in order to build the runway. It reads:
Fisheries studies just being made public disclose that a significant number of young Chinook salmon fingerlings spend up to six months in the shallows of Sturgeon Bank after coming down the Fraser River and before journeying further in their life cycle; obviously, the salmon fishery would be seriously affected by the land fill on Sturgeon Bank proposed in the expansion.
That is just one matter which has to be studied before we really know whether we should go ahead with this runway. As a consequence of that and of other matters which have been raised and debated in this House, I ask these questions: Can these studies in fact be prepared in 12 months? We have found out recently in the Squamish area, in the province of British Columbia, that in fact salmon migrating downstream do spend time in the mouths of rivers. This seems to be something we did not know before. I do not know how many other things in connection with the fishery run in the Fraser River we should know before we build the runway.
What assurance do we have that if proper studies are not done, the airport expansion will not be undertaken until the studies are completed? Under what legislation will this study promised by the minister be done, if any legislation does exist, and will there be public hearings? Will there be an opportunity for the public to take part, are we going to be faced with the situation where we have an entirely ad hoc response by the government as a result of the political pressures brought to bear here in the House of Commons during the past month or two?
I know that I speak for many people in this House when I say that we want answers to these questions. We want these promised hearings and studies to take place under proper circumstances, with the maximum of public input, and not rushed to meet the construction deadline, so that
Adjournment Debate
we will have sufficient information to know whether the construction should proceed at all.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Phillipe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-PROPOSED NEW RUNWAY-REQUEST FOR INFORMATION ON ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) I should like to quote the three ministers who said that if, after reviewing the hearing officer's report, the federal government decided to proceed with a second new parallel runway for the Vancouver international airport, no construction would take place until a full 12-month environmental study had been completed and was made public. This release was made by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis), the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand).
I should like to add that the Minister of Transport has stated that following a review of the hearing officer's report concerning the intended expropriation of land required for the expansion of Vancouver international airport, the federal government has decided that it will proceed to complete the acquisition of the necessary land on Sea Island.
The Minister of Transport stated that Vancouver international airport is the springboard for Canada and the Pacific rim countries, and as such is an essential facility in Canada's air transportation network. The Minister of Transport expressed his deep concern about the property owners involved and the feelings they expressed. The minister stated that the rights of property owners to full and fair compensation could best be provided under the terms of the expropriation act.
The hon. minister also stated that the government would ensure that the expansion of the airport facilities would not be undertaken without full consideration of the impact on the urban and natural environment, and the studies involved would be made public and freely discussed. Further, to ensure that federal plans are coordinated with the activities of other levels of government and that public concerns are taken fully into account, the minister announced that the topic of airport expansion, if other levels of government agree, would be placed on the agenda, on a continuing basis, of the greater Vancouver tri-level committee.
The proposed tri-level committee group for greater Vancouver will bring together political leaders and officials of the federal government, the province and the greater Vancouver regional district. Regular meetings would be held to discuss a wide range of urban issues involving consultation and co-ordination among the governments. In addition to airport expansion, other issues which could be placed on the tri-level agenda include urban growth patterns-which includes the question raised this evening- and the whole question of transportation patterns and facilities for the lower mainland and connections with Vancouver Island.
